# Page: Overview

# Overview

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

Transformers is a model-definition framework for machine learning across text, computer vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks. It supports both inference and training, and is designed to provide model definitions that can be agreed upon and reused across the broader machine-learning ecosystem [README.md:70-80](). This page introduces the library’s purpose and major subsystems; use the linked child pages for installation, design details, and documentation conventions.

Sources: [README.md:70-80]()

## Design Philosophy

Transformers centralizes model definitions so they can be seamlessly integrated into training frameworks, inference engines, and adjacent modeling libraries [README.md:73-80](). Its public namespace exposes subsystem APIs—including generation, pipelines, preprocessing, and training utilities—through a deferred import structure [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-99](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-179]().

The repository organizes model implementations under `src/transformers/models/`, with model modules included through generated package exports [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:1-5](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-43](). For details on the single-file-per-model approach, composition, and v5 migration, see [Design Philosophy & V5 Migration Guide](#1.2).

Sources: [README.md:73-80](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-99](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-179](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:1-5](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-43]()

## Key Subsystems Overview

The library combines model architectures and configuration with automatic class resolution, input processing, generation, pipelines, and training-related APIs. The package import structure lists public names for these areas, while model and tokenizer auto mappings connect model types to concrete implementations [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-99](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-185](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78]().

| Subsystem | Role at a glance |
|---|---|
| Model architectures | Model families are organized in `src/transformers/models/`; the generated model package exports their modules [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:1-5](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-43](). |
| Auto factories | Mappings associate model types with model, configuration, and tokenizer classes [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:34-48](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78](). |
| Input processing | The public API includes tokenizer, feature-extraction, and processor-related names [src/transformers/__init__.py:86-88](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:150-170](). |
| Generation and pipelines | Generation configuration and streamers, plus task-oriented pipeline APIs, are part of the public import structure [src/transformers/__init__.py:89-98](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-149](). |
| Training | The public API includes callback and training utility names [src/transformers/__init__.py:171-185](). |

Sources: [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-99](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-185](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:1-5](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-43](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:34-48](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78]()

## System Architecture: Bridging Concepts with Code Entities

### Model selection and input-processing map

This high-level map connects common library concepts to named mapping structures and package APIs. Auto mappings associate model types with implementation names; the top-level package exposes pipeline, processor, and generation APIs [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:89-98](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-157]().

**Diagram: From model type to public APIs**

```mermaid
graph TD
    Concept["Select model and prepare inputs"] --> Config["CONFIG_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    Concept --> Model["MODEL_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    Concept --> Tokenizer["TOKENIZER_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    Model --> Architecture["src/transformers/models/"]
    Tokenizer --> Input["PreTrainedTokenizerBase and BatchEncoding"]
    Input --> Processor["ProcessorMixin"]
    Architecture --> Pipeline["pipeline and Pipeline"]
    Processor --> Pipeline
    Pipeline --> Generation["GenerationConfig and streamers"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:34-48](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:89-98](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-157](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:160-168]()

### Natural language concepts and repository entities

This second map provides repository search terms for major concepts. For example, model-family names appear in auto mappings, while `pipeline`, `GenerationConfig`, and `TrainerCallback` are among the public package exports [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:89-98](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-149](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:171-179]().

**Diagram: Concepts mapped to code names**

```mermaid
graph LR
    Models["Model architectures"] --> Mapping["MODEL_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    Mapping --> Example["albert to AlbertModel"]
    Example --> ModelPackage["src/transformers/models/"]
    Input["Text input"] --> TokenMap["TOKENIZER_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    TokenMap --> TokenBase["PreTrainedTokenizerBase"]
    Multimodal["Multimodal input"] --> ProcessorMixin["ProcessorMixin"]
    Inference["Task inference"] --> Pipeline["pipeline and Pipeline"]
    Generation["Text generation"] --> GenerationConfig["GenerationConfig"]
    Training["Training utilities"] --> Callback["TrainerCallback"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-78](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:89-98](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:117-157](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:160-168](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:171-179]()

# Page: Getting Started & Installation

# Getting Started & Installation

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.python-version](.python-version)
- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page covers the repository’s installation metadata, optional dependency groups, dependency-version synchronization, and the documented first-inference path using `pipeline`. It distinguishes package-installation configuration from development-tool configuration: `setup.py` defines dependencies and extras, `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py` is generated from that dependency list, and `pyproject.toml` configures tools such as Ruff and pytest. [setup.py:50-72]()[src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4]()[pyproject.toml:16-18]()[pyproject.toml:84-101]()

Sources: `setup.py:50-72`, `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4`, `pyproject.toml:16-18`, `pyproject.toml:84-101`

---

## Environment Setup

The setup script declares a supported Python minor-version range of 3.11 through 3.14 and records the current interpreter’s minor version for conditional extra construction. [setup.py:50-54]() The displayed setup code removes a stale `transformers.egg-info` directory before packaging, noting that it can interfere with editable installation. [setup.py:55-66]() [.python-version:1-1]()

The repository’s quickstart documents installing PyTorch and then installing Transformers and related ecosystem packages. Its example uses `datasets`, `evaluate`, `accelerate`, and `timm` alongside Transformers. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:58-70]() The specific backend and optional dependencies you need depend on the models and tasks you plan to use; the package extras described below provide named groups for several common requirements. [setup.py:167-194]()

| Setup concern | Repository implementation |
|---|---|
| Python support | `SUPPORTED_PYTHON_VERSIONS` is `(11, 14)`; `PYTHON_MINOR_VERSION` is used in conditional extra definitions. [setup.py:50-54]() |
| Editable-install cleanup | A stale `transformers.egg-info` directory is detected and removed. [setup.py:55-66]() |
| Dependency source | `_deps` contains package requirements and version constraints. [setup.py:69-72]() |
| Local repository imports | The Makefile sets `PYTHONPATH = src` for its commands. [Makefile:1-4]() |

Sources: `setup.py:50-72`, `.python-version:1-1`, `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:58-70`, `Makefile:1-4`

---

## Core Dependencies

The `_deps` list in `setup.py` is the declared dependency inventory. Its entries include package names with optional version constraints; the setup script comments that dependency changes should be followed by `make fix-repo` to update the generated dependency table. [setup.py:69-72]() The list includes, among others, `torch`, `accelerate`, `huggingface-hub`, `tokenizers`, and `safetensors`, with constraints shown in the source. [setup.py:72-156]()

| Dependency | Declared requirement | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `python` | `python>=3.11.0` | The supported minor range is separately recorded as 3.11–3.14. [setup.py:50-54]()[setup.py:118-118]() |
| `torch` | `torch>=2.6` | Listed in `_deps`; also included in the `torch` extra. [setup.py:142-142]()[setup.py:167-170]() |
| `accelerate` | `accelerate>=1.1.0` | Listed in `_deps` and grouped with `torch` in the `torch` extra. [setup.py:74-74]()[setup.py:169-169]() |
| `huggingface-hub` | `huggingface-hub>=1.31.0,<3.0` | Listed in `_deps`. [setup.py:88-88]() |
| `tokenizers` | `tokenizers>=0.23.1,<0.24.0` | Listed in `_deps`. [setup.py:141-141]() |
| `safetensors` | `safetensors>=0.8.0` | Listed in `_deps`. [setup.py:128-128]() |
| `numpy` | `numpy>=1.17` | Listed in `_deps`. [setup.py:97-97]() |
| `Pillow` | `Pillow>=10.0.1,<=15.0` | Also included in the `vision` extra. [setup.py:73-73]()[setup.py:170-170]() |

Sources: `setup.py:50-54`, `setup.py:69-156`, `setup.py:167-170`

## Installation via Optional Extras

`setup.py` creates a `deps` lookup from `_deps`, then defines `deps_list()` to retrieve the corresponding requirement strings by package key. The `extras` dictionary uses this helper to define named optional dependency groups. [setup.py:158-165]()[setup.py:167-194]()

| Extra | Dependencies grouped by the setup script |
|---|---|
| `torch` | `torch`, `accelerate`. [setup.py:169-169]() |
| `vision` | `torchvision`, `Pillow`. [setup.py:170-170]() |
| `audio` | `torchaudio`, `librosa`, `pyctcdecode`, `phonemizer`; `kenlm` is added when the Python minor version is less than 13. [setup.py:171-173]() |
| `video` | `av`. [setup.py:174-174]() |
| `timm` | `timm`. [setup.py:175-175]() |
| `quality` | `datasets`, `ruff`, `GitPython`, `urllib3`, `libcst`, `rich`, `ty`, and `transformers-mlinter`. [setup.py:176-178]() |
| `docs` | `hf-doc-builder`. [setup.py:179-179]() |
| `kernels` | `kernels`. [setup.py:180-180]() |
| `sentencepiece` | `sentencepiece`, `protobuf`. [setup.py:181-181]() |
| `tiktoken` | `tiktoken`, `blobfile`. [setup.py:182-182]() |
| `mistral-common` | `mistral-common[image]`. [setup.py:183-183]() |
| `chat_template` | `jinja2`. [setup.py:184-184]() |
| `sklearn` | `scikit-learn`. [setup.py:185-185]() |
| `accelerate` | `accelerate`. [setup.py:186-186]() |
| `retrieval` | `faiss-cpu`, `datasets`. [setup.py:187-187]() |
| `sagemaker` | `sagemaker`. [setup.py:188-188]() |
| `deepspeed` | `deepspeed`, `accelerate`. [setup.py:189-189]() |
| `optuna` | `optuna`. [setup.py:190-190]() |
| `integrations` | `kernels`, `optuna`, `codecarbon`, and, when Python is below 3.14, the `ray` extra. [setup.py:191-194]() |

The extra definitions use requirements from the `deps` mapping rather than duplicating version strings in each group. [setup.py:158-165]()

Sources: `setup.py:158-194`

### Installing extras

Extras are named groups in the package metadata. For example, the repository’s CI configuration installs the editable checkout with the `quality` extra; the quickstart separately documents installing PyTorch and the Transformers ecosystem packages. [setup.py:167-194]()[.circleci/config.yml:100-118]()[docs/source/en/quicktour.md:58-70]()

Sources: `setup.py:167-194`, `.circleci/config.yml:100-118`, `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:58-70`

## Dependency Versioning & Synchronization

The dependency table is generated metadata, not a separate place to define requirements. Its header instructs maintainers to modify `_deps` in `setup.py` and run `make fix-repo`; the generated `deps` dictionary maps dependency keys to requirement strings. [src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4]() The setup script likewise calls out `make fix-repo` as the step for updating this file when dependencies change. [setup.py:69-72]()

The Makefile defines `fix-repo` as a repository-checker invocation with automatic fixes enabled. [Makefile:58-64]() The repository’s checker list includes `deps_table`, linking the generated dependency table to repository consistency checks. [Makefile:17-39]()

### Dependency synchronization flow

**Diagram: Dependency declaration to generated table**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SetupDeps["_deps in setup.py"] -->|"make fix-repo"| FixRepo["Makefile fix-repo"]
    FixRepo -->|"runs repository checkers with --fix"| Checkers["utils/checkers.py"]
    Checkers -->|"updates generated dependency data"| VersionTable["dependency_versions_table.py deps"]
```

Sources: `setup.py:69-72`, `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4`, `Makefile:58-64`

### Packaging and development configuration

`setup.py` contains the dependency and extras definitions discussed above. [setup.py:69-194]() `pyproject.toml` configures development tools: it sets Ruff’s target Python version and line length, defines lint and formatting rules, and configures pytest options such as Markdown doctest discovery. [pyproject.toml:16-18]()[pyproject.toml:20-79]()[pyproject.toml:84-101]() These pytest and lint settings are repository tooling configuration; they are not the source of the package extras. [setup.py:69-194]()[pyproject.toml:16-18]()[pyproject.toml:84-101]()

| File | Role in this page |
|---|---|
| `setup.py` | Supported Python range, dependency requirements, and optional extras. [setup.py:50-72]()[setup.py:158-194]() |
| `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py` | Autogenerated dependency mapping; its header points back to `setup.py` and `make fix-repo`. [src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4]() |
| `pyproject.toml` | Ruff and pytest configuration. [pyproject.toml:16-18]()[pyproject.toml:84-101]() |
| `Makefile` | Defines `fix-repo` and the checker list, including `deps_table`. [Makefile:17-39]()[Makefile:58-64]() |

Sources: `setup.py:50-72`, `setup.py:158-194`, `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4`, `pyproject.toml:16-18`, `pyproject.toml:84-101`, `Makefile:17-39`, `Makefile:58-64`

## First Inference: Running Your First Pipeline

The quickstart identifies `Pipeline` as the convenient high-level API for inference and lists tasks including text generation, image segmentation, automatic speech recognition, and document question answering. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156]() It explains that a pipeline is created for a task and that a default pretrained model is downloaded and cached unless a model is specified. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156]()

A pipeline example should be understood as an API-level workflow: choose a task and model, provide input, and receive task-formatted results. The detailed task routing and pipeline construction implementation is outside the supplied source excerpts, so this page does not attribute specific internal calls to `pipeline()`. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156]()

### Natural-Language Task to Code Entity (API Mapping)

**Diagram: User task mapped to documented API concepts**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    UserIntent["Run text generation"] --> TaskName["text-generation"]
    TaskName --> PipelineAPI["Pipeline"]
    ModelChoice["Pretrained model name or default"] --> PipelineAPI
    PipelineAPI --> Inference["Task inference"]
```

Sources: `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156`

### Inference Data Flow

For direct model use, the quickstart describes loading a pretrained model and tokenizer with Auto classes, tokenizing input into PyTorch tensors, moving inputs to the model’s device, generating token IDs, and decoding those IDs back to text. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:114-144]() This path exposes the processing stages explicitly; `Pipeline` offers a higher-level inference interface. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:130-144]()[docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156]()

**Diagram: Quickstart model-inference path mapped to code entities**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    TextInput["Text input"] --> AutoTokenizer["AutoTokenizer"]
    AutoTokenizer --> ModelInputs["return_tensors=pt"]
    ModelInputs --> AutoModel["AutoModelForCausalLM"]
    AutoModel --> Generate["generate"]
    Generate --> TokenIDs["generated token IDs"]
    TokenIDs --> BatchDecode["batch_decode"]
    BatchDecode --> TextOutput["Decoded text"]
```

Sources: `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:123-144`

### Pipeline First-Use Notes

The quickstart states that `Pipeline` supports multiple tasks and that a task’s default pretrained model is used when no model is specified; users can specify a model name to choose one. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156]() Consult the pipeline API reference for the supported task list, as directed by the quickstart. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:151-156]()

Sources: `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:149-156`

## Repository Structure & Metadata Management

### `setup.py`

`setup.py` records the supported Python minor-version range, performs stale `transformers.egg-info` cleanup, defines `_deps`, constructs the `deps` lookup and helper, and assembles named extras. [setup.py:50-72]()[setup.py:158-194]()

Sources: `setup.py:50-72`, `setup.py:158-194`

### `dependency_versions_table.py`

`src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py` is marked autogenerated. Its header identifies `_deps` in `setup.py` as the source and `make fix-repo` as the update procedure; the file contains a `deps` dictionary of requirement strings. [src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-86]()

Sources: `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-86`

### `pyproject.toml`

`pyproject.toml` configures Ruff, including its target version, line length, lint rules, and formatting settings. [pyproject.toml:16-79]() It also configures pytest, including Markdown doctest discovery, doctest options, markers, logging, and environment settings. [pyproject.toml:84-114]()

Sources: `pyproject.toml:16-79`, `pyproject.toml:84-114`

---

## Summary

- The setup script declares Python support from 3.11 through 3.14 and maintains the dependency requirements in `_deps`. [setup.py:50-54]()[setup.py:69-156]()
- Optional groups such as `torch`, `vision`, `audio`, `video`, `quality`, and `sentencepiece` are assembled through the `extras` dictionary. [setup.py:167-194]()
- `dependency_versions_table.py` is generated from the dependency declarations; `make fix-repo` runs the repository checkers with fixes enabled. [src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4]()[Makefile:58-64]()
- `pyproject.toml` configures development tools, including Ruff and pytest. [pyproject.toml:16-79]()[pyproject.toml:84-114]()
- The quickstart documents both the high-level `Pipeline` inference API and the explicit tokenizer-to-generation-to-decoding workflow. [docs/source/en/quicktour.md:123-156]()

Sources: `setup.py:50-54`, `setup.py:69-156`, `setup.py:167-194`, `src/transformers/dependency_versions_table.py:1-4`, `Makefile:58-64`, `pyproject.toml:16-79`, `pyproject.toml:84-114`, `docs/source/en/quicktour.md:123-156`, `README.md:1-137`

# Page: Design Philosophy & V5 Migration Guide

# Design Philosophy & V5 Migration Guide

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md](MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the model-file organization and code-generation approach documented for Transformers, and summarizes the v5 migration changes covered by the supplied migration guide: removal of TensorFlow and JAX implementations, tokenizer backend consolidation, and dynamic weight loading. The available sources do not document the full implementation details of model composition or the internal call graph of the weight-loading API, so those topics are limited to what the sources establish. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:17-75]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:17-75]()

---

## Design Philosophy

The model organization described here aims to retain standalone model files for users while allowing contributors to reuse code when implementing related architectures. The modular Transformers workflow provides inheritance and code generation as a contributor-facing option; the generated files preserve the familiar standalone interface. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25]()

### 1. Single-File-per-Model

A model’s generated, standalone implementation is organized in the model’s directory. The modular workflow uses `modular_<name>.py` as an optional contributor source and generates standalone files from it. Contributors can also write a `modeling.py` file manually when the model does not build cleanly on existing implementations. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

This separates contributor implementation choices from the interface users encounter: contributors may use modular inheritance, while generated output retains the standalone-file convention. The guide does not require every model to use the modular workflow. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

### 2. Composition, Reuse, and Bounded Abstraction

The available implementation guidance supports reuse through inheritance in modular files, but also sets limits on that reuse. Contributors should find a similar model and inherit from existing classes where appropriate; they should not modify an existing model merely to make inheritance possible. If renaming or subclassing a parent is awkward, copying the relevant code is an acceptable alternative. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:27-45]()

Thus, the documented approach is not “abstract everything.” It permits reuse when it fits the architecture and favors direct, standalone implementation when a clean inheritance relationship is not available. The provided material does not specify how individual model heads compose base models internally, so no universal rule about their `forward()` implementations is asserted here. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:22-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:42-45]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:22-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:27-45]()

### 3. Modular Source and Generated Output

A modular file lives in the model directory and can inherit from existing model components. A converter generates standalone files from that modular source, so users continue to work with the familiar single-file interface. The documentation identifies `modular_<name>.py` as the source filename pattern and describes manual `modeling.py` implementation as an option for models that cannot cleanly inherit from an existing implementation. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

The supplied documentation does not give the converter’s implementation path or define its full generation algorithm. Accordingly, this page describes the workflow without assigning unsupported details to specific converter functions or classes. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

### Diagram: Contributor Intent to Standalone Model Files

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ContributorChoosesModularReuse"] --> B["modular_<name>.py"]
    A --> C["ManualModelingPyWhenInheritanceDoesNotFit"]
    B --> D["ConverterGeneratesStandaloneFiles"]
    D --> E["UserFacingStandaloneModelFiles"]
    C --> E
```

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

---

## V5 Migration: Core Changes

The v5 migration guide describes two library-wide changes relevant to this page: removing TensorFlow and JAX implementations in order to focus on `torch`, and introducing a new weight-loading API for applying transformations to checkpoints. It also describes tokenizer backend consolidation. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:19-39](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:19-39](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]()

### Removal of TensorFlow and JAX Support

The migration guide states that the TensorFlow and JAX parts of the library are being removed so development can focus on `torch` as the backend. It describes the expected benefit as reduced model-maintenance cost. It also notes that Transformers is working with tools in the JAX ecosystem, such as MaxText, to explore compatibility while keeping `torch` as the only backend for now. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:21-28]()

| Migration point | Documented direction |
|---|---|
| TensorFlow and JAX implementations | Removal from the library |
| Backend focus | `torch` as the only backend for now |
| JAX ecosystem interaction | Compatibility work with tools such as MaxText |

[MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:21-28]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:21-28]()

### Tokenizer Backend Consolidation

Before v5, the migration guide describes two parallel tokenizer implementations: Python-based “slow” tokenizers in `tokenization_<model>.py`, and Rust-backed “fast” tokenizers in `tokenization_<model>_fast.py`. The v5 direction is a single `tokenization_<model>.py` file per model, using an appropriate backend. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-128]()

The guide lists four backend options:

| Backend | Role described in the migration guide |
|---|---|
| `TokenizersBackend` | Preferred Rust-based backend using the Hugging Face `tokenizers` library; supports features including added-token handling, a Python API, parallelization, offsets, customization, and training. |
| `SentencePieceBackend` | Backend for tokenizers requiring the `sentencepiece` library; inherits from `PythonBackend`. |
| `PythonBackend` | Python implementation of features provided by `tokenizers`, including the ability to add tokens. |
| `MistralCommonBackend` | Backend relying on the MistralCommon tokenization library. |

[MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:126-138]()

`AutoTokenizer` is described as selecting the appropriate backend based on available files and dependencies. The migration guide states that callers continue to use `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained()` as before; backend selection is intended to be transparent to them. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:139-139]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]()

### Diagram: Tokenizer Files and Backend Selection

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained()"] --> B["AvailableFilesAndDependencies"]
    B --> C["AutoTokenizerBackendSelection"]
    C --> D["TokenizersBackend"]
    C --> E["SentencePieceBackend"]
    C --> F["PythonBackend"]
    C --> G["MistralCommonBackend"]
    H["tokenization_<model>.py"] --> C
```

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]()

---

## Dynamic Weight Loading API

The migration guide introduces a new weight-loading API centered on `WeightConverter` [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-46](). Its stated purpose is to apply operations to checkpoints as Transformers loads them, rather than requiring checkpoint tensors to be loaded exactly as serialized. The operations can reshape, merge, or split layers to match how the model layers are defined. The guide identifies quantization and parallelism algorithms as use cases for such transformations. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:30-39]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:30-39]()

### `WeightConverter` and Conversion Operations

The guide describes `WeightConverter` as carrying a list of `ConversionOps`, source key or keys, and target key or keys [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:42-46](). In the documented flow, operations act on the source keys and produce the target keys [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:48-51]().

| Concept | Role |
|---|---|
| `WeightConverter` | Defines a conversion from checkpoint source keys to model target keys [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-46](). |
| `source_keys` | The input checkpoint key or keys for the conversion [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:44-44](). |
| `target_keys` | The resulting model key or keys [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:45-45](). |
| `operations` | Operations applied to the source layer tensors to produce the target layer tensors [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:33-36](). |
| `Concatenate` | Example operation that combines a list of layers into one layer [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:56-60](). |

[MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-61]()

The guide says that a mapping from architecture to weight conversions can apply transformations to layers and that this simplifies `from_pretrained`. It does not specify the implementation call sites or the complete inventory of conversion operations in the provided excerpt. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:63-65]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-65]()

### Example Transformation: QKV Fusion

The migration guide’s example maps the three attention projection keys `self_attn.q_proj`, `self_attn.k_proj`, and `self_attn.v_proj` to `self_attn.qkv_proj` [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:53-55](). It uses `Concatenate(dim=0)` to combine the source layers into a single output layer [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:56-56]().

This illustrates the data transformation at the level described by the guide: several checkpoint tensors become one target tensor through an explicit operation. The example does not establish that every model uses fused QKV projections. [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:48-61]()

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:48-61]()

### Diagram: Checkpoint Keys to `WeightConverter` Targets

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["self_attn.q_proj"] --> D["WeightConverter"]
    B["self_attn.k_proj"] --> D
    C["self_attn.v_proj"] --> D
    D --> E["Concatenate(dim=0)"]
    E --> F["self_attn.qkv_proj"]
```

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-61]()

### Intended Benefits and Rollout Caveat

The migration guide lists the intended benefits of the new API as cleaner transformation definitions, reversible transformations so loading and saving should preserve the checkpoint, faster loading through scheduled tensor materialization, and support for complex combinations such as quantization with MoEs or tensor parallelism with MoEs [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:67-71](). The guide cautions that support may vary across release candidates while the API is being implemented [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:73-73]().

Sources: [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:63-75]()

---

## Modular Transformers System

The modular workflow addresses reuse between related models while preserving standalone generated files. Contributors add `modular_<name>.py` in the model folder and use inheritance to share or specialize components; a converter generates standalone files from that source. The documentation describes modular Transformers as an option, not a replacement for legacy modeling code. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

A contributor should choose a parent model only when its implementation is a suitable fit. The guide explicitly recommends copying relevant code rather than forcing inheritance when renaming or subclassing would be awkward. It also notes that contributors may start from a modular file or begin with a hand-written `modeling.py` and refactor later. [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:22-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:27-45]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:27-47]()

### Diagram: Modular Model Workflow Mapped to Code Entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["src/transformers/models/<name>/"] --> B["modular_<name>.py"]
    B --> C["ExistingModelClassesAndImports"]
    B --> D["Converter"]
    D --> E["StandaloneGeneratedModelFiles"]
    F["ManualModelingPy"] --> E
    E --> G["UserFacingModelInterface"]
```

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]()

---

## Summary Table

| Topic | Summary | Code entities and paths |
|---|---|---|
| Standalone model files | Modular sources can generate standalone files; manual implementation remains supported when inheritance does not fit. | `modular_<name>.py`, `modeling.py` [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:18-25](), [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:45-47]() |
| Reuse strategy | Inherit from suitable existing components; avoid changing a parent solely to enable inheritance; copy relevant code when inheritance is awkward. | Existing model classes and imports [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:27-45]() |
| v5 backend direction | The migration guide describes removal of TensorFlow and JAX implementations and a focus on `torch`. | `torch`, MaxText [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:21-28]() |
| Tokenizer consolidation | One `tokenization_<model>.py` file selects an appropriate backend; `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained()` remains the user-facing entry point. | `TokenizersBackend`, `SentencePieceBackend`, `PythonBackend`, `MistralCommonBackend`, `AutoTokenizer` [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]() |
| Dynamic weight loading | `WeightConverter` applies `ConversionOps` from source keys to target keys, with QKV concatenation as an example. | `WeightConverter`, `ConversionOps`, `Concatenate` [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:39-61]() |
| Migration status | The guide notes that support levels may vary across release candidates during implementation. | v5 weight-loading API [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:73-75]() |

Sources: [docs/source/en/modular_transformers.md:16-47](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:19-75](), [MIGRATION_GUIDE_V5.md:120-140]()

# Documentation Structure & Translations

This page (Section 1.3) describes how the supplied documentation files organize localized navigation, identify model documentation in the table of contents, guide translation work, and connect documentation sources to automated build workflows. The examples below reflect the files provided; they do not imply that every language has identical content or that the workflows build every language. Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:1-47](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:1-28](), [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:1-61](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:1-49]()

## 1. Documentation Tree Organization per Language

The provided language-specific navigation files include `docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml`, `docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml`, and `docs/source/es/_toctree.yml`. Each uses YAML entries with `sections`, `local`, and `title` fields to describe navigation. The `local` values identify pages or nested paths within that language’s documentation source; `title` supplies the displayed, localized label. Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:1-8](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:1-8](), [docs/source/es/_toctree.yml:1-8]()

The files show that navigation is localized and need not have identical structure:

| Language file | Examples from the supplied navigation |
|---|---|
| Korean, `docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml` | `index`, `installation`, and `quicktour` appear under `시작하기`; nested sections include model and preprocessing topics. |
| Chinese, `docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml` | `index`, `quicktour`, and `installation` appear under `开始使用`; separate top-level groups include tutorials and developer guides. |
| Spanish, `docs/source/es/_toctree.yml` | `index`, `quicktour`, and `installation` appear under `Empezar`; other groups include tutorials and practical guides. |

Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:1-8](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:1-28](), [docs/source/es/_toctree.yml:1-51]()

Korean navigation also uses `isExpanded: false` for some groups and routes untranslated entries to `in_translation`, with a localized title indicating translation is in progress. For example, the table of contents includes untranslated model-documentation and video-processor topics. Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:9-28](), [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:29-46]()

### Diagram: Localized navigation entries and page references

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  KO["_toctree.yml: docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml"] --> KO_GROUP["sections: 시작하기"]
  KO_GROUP --> KO_INDEX["local: index"]
  KO_GROUP --> KO_INSTALL["local: installation"]
  KO["docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml"] --> KO_MODEL["sections: 모델"]
  KO_MODEL --> KO_PAGE["local: models"]
  KO_MODEL --> KO_PENDING["local: in_translation"]
  ZH["_toctree.yml: docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml"] --> ZH_GROUP["sections: 开始使用"]
  ZH_GROUP --> ZH_INDEX["local: index"]
  ZH["_toctree.yml: docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml"] --> ZH_TUTORIALS["sections: 教程"]
```

Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:1-28](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:1-28]()

## 2. Model Documentation Convention: `model_doc`

The supplied Chinese table of contents places `local: model_doc/bert` inside the API section’s internal-helper navigation group. This demonstrates that a model-specific page can be referenced using the `model_doc/...` path convention. The Korean table of contents separately contains an `in_translation` entry titled “Documenting a model”; this is an untranslated navigation entry, not a `model_doc` path. Sources: [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:143-165](), [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:20-27]()

Additional files in the supplied cluster include `docs/source/zh/model_doc/bert.md`, `docs/source/ko/model_doc/albert.md`, and Japanese model documentation files. Their inclusion in the file list establishes examples of language-specific `model_doc` paths, but the contents of those pages were not provided here. Sources: [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:162-165]()

## 3. Internationalization (i18n) Helper READMEs

The `i18n/` directory contains language-specific README files. The supplied examples include `i18n/README_zh-hans.md`, `i18n/README_ja.md`, and `i18n/README_fr.md`. These READMEs include language selectors linking to other README translations. Sources: [i18n/README_zh-hans.md:17-40](), [i18n/README_zh-hans.md:62-85](), [i18n/README_ja.md:17-50](), [i18n/README_fr.md:17-59]()

The Simplified Chinese and Japanese READMEs include translation guidance in HTML comments. The Chinese guide gives spacing and quotation-mark guidance and a terminology dictionary; the Japanese guide provides a terminology dictionary and quotation-mark guidance. These are README translation guidelines, not evidence of automated translation or of a single shared glossary format. Sources: [i18n/README_zh-hans.md:17-40](), [i18n/README_ja.md:17-50]()

The README language selectors also illustrate the translation set. For example, the Chinese and French files link to README translations for languages including Korean, Spanish, Japanese, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and others. Sources: [i18n/README_zh-hans.md:62-85](), [i18n/README_fr.md:36-59]()

```mermaid
  ZH --> ZH_TERMS["Terminology dictionary"]

```

## 4. Documentation Build Workflows

The supplied GitHub Actions configuration shows distinct workflows for PR documentation checks, comment-triggered PR builds, and documentation builds on selected pushes or manual dispatch. These workflows call reusable workflows from `huggingface/doc-builder`; the supplied configuration does not specify the internal rendering implementation, the full set of languages built, or the final deployment process. Sources: [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:1-61](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:1-49]()

### 4.1. PR documentation workflow: `build_pr_documentation.yml`

The workflow is triggered by `pull_request` and `merge_group`. For pull requests, its `check_links` job reads the Python version from `.python-version`, installs `doc-builder`, and runs `doc-builder check-links docs/source/en`. The `build` job depends on `check_links` and calls the reusable PR documentation workflow with the package name `transformers` and `path_to_docs: transformers/docs/source/en/`. For merge-queue events, `skip_merge_queue` skips the documentation build; `doc_build_status_check` evaluates the job results. Sources: [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:1-20](), [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:27-61](), [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:63-84]()

### 4.2. Main documentation workflow: `build_documentation.yml`

This workflow runs on `workflow_dispatch` and pushes to the listed branches: `main`, `doc-builder*`, `v*-release`, and `use_templates`. It reads `.python-version` and calls the reusable `build_main_documentation.yml` workflow with the commit SHA, package `transformers`, notebook folder `transformers_doc`, and documentation path `transformers/docs/source/en/`. The provided configuration specifies the English documentation path; it does not provide a list of additional languages. Sources: [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:1-10](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:16-49]()

### 4.3. Build workflow data flow

The documented workflow configuration gives the following high-level flow: workflow event → Python version and commit inputs → reusable `huggingface/doc-builder` workflow. PR workflows additionally run an English link check in `build_pr_documentation.yml`; the main workflow passes the English docs path to its reusable workflow. Sources: [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:14-61](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:16-49]()

### Diagram: Events and configured documentation workflow paths

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  PR["pull_request event"] --> PR_LINKS["check_links"]
  PR_LINKS --> LINK_COMMAND["doc-builder check-links docs/source/en"]
  PR_LINKS --> PR_BUILD["build"]
  PR_BUILD --> PR_REUSABLE["Reusable build_pr_documentation.yml"]
  PR_REUSABLE --> PR_PATH["transformers/docs/source/en/"]
  PUSH["push to configured branches"] --> MAIN_BUILD["build_documentation.yml"]
  DISPATCH["workflow_dispatch"] --> MAIN_BUILD
  MAIN_BUILD --> MAIN_REUSABLE["Reusable build_main_documentation.yml"]
  MAIN_REUSABLE --> MAIN_PATH["transformers/docs/source/en/"]
```

Sources: [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:1-61](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:1-49]()

## 7. Connecting Natural Language Space to Code Entity Space

A navigation title is the reader-facing label; the `local` value is the repository-facing page identifier. The Chinese table of contents demonstrates this mapping for BERT: a human-readable title, `BERT`, points to `local: model_doc/bert`. The same file also organizes this entry under `API` and `Internal helpers` sections. Sources: [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:108-165]()

### Diagram: Reader-facing BERT entry mapped to navigation entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  NATURAL["Natural language: BERT model documentation"] --> API_TITLE["title: 应用程序接口 (API)"]
  API_TITLE --> INTERNAL_TITLE["title: 内部辅助工具"]
  INTERNAL_TITLE --> MODEL_LOCAL["local: model_doc/bert"]
  MODEL_LOCAL --> MODEL_PATH["docs/source/zh/model_doc/bert.md"]
  MODEL_PATH --> MODEL_EXAMPLE["Model page example: BERT"]
```

Sources: [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:143-165]()

The build workflow configuration similarly maps an operational concept—checking documentation links—to concrete workflow entities: the `check_links` job, its `doc-builder check-links docs/source/en` command, and the configured documentation path passed to the reusable build. The reusable workflow is referenced by its workflow path and inputs; its implementation is not included in the supplied files. Sources: [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:14-20](), [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:44-61]()

### Diagram: Link-checking intent mapped to workflow entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  NATURAL["Natural language: validate PR documentation links"] --> JOB["job: check_links"]
  JOB --> INSTALL["Install doc-builder"]
  JOB --> FUNCTION["Command: doc-builder check-links docs/source/en"]
  JOB --> BUILD_JOB["job: build"]
  BUILD_JOB --> REUSABLE["huggingface/doc-builder build_pr_documentation.yml"]
```

## Summary

The supplied documentation navigation files use language-specific `_toctree.yml` files with localized `title` values and `local` page references. Their structures vary across the Korean, Chinese, and Spanish examples; Korean also includes entries marked `in_translation`. The Chinese table of contents demonstrates a `model_doc/bert` navigation entry, while the supplied file list includes additional language-specific model-documentation paths. Sources: [docs/source/ko/_toctree.yml:1-47](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:1-28](), [docs/source/es/_toctree.yml:1-51](), [docs/source/zh/_toctree.yml:143-165]()

The supplied i18n READMEs provide language-specific translation guidance and terminology examples. Documentation workflows use `huggingface/doc-builder` reusable workflows: PR validation includes an English link check and PR build, while the main workflow passes the English docs path to its reusable build. Sources: [i18n/README_zh-hans.md:17-40](), [i18n/README_ja.md:17-50](), [.github/workflows/build_pr_documentation.yml:39-61](), [.github/workflows/build_documentation.yml:38-49]()

# Page: Core Architecture

# Core Architecture

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This parent page maps the foundational abstractions used across Transformers models: configuration and model base classes, Auto factories, checkpoint conversion, and shared modeling utilities. It gives a high-level view and links to child pages for implementation details. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:49-56]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:49-56]()

---

## Foundational Abstractions

### `PreTrainedConfig`

`PreTrainedConfig` is referenced by `modeling_utils.py` as the configuration type used alongside the base model machinery. The configuration and model abstractions connect model-specific settings with model implementations; see [PreTrainedModel & PreTrainedConfig](#2.1) for the configuration lifecycle and serialization details. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:48-50]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:48-50]()

### `PreTrainedModel`

`PreTrainedModel` is the shared model abstraction. Its implementation brings together weight conversion and loading, distributed support, quantization, attention integrations, and other modeling utilities. For details about the model lifecycle and individual capabilities, see [PreTrainedModel & PreTrainedConfig](#2.1). [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:46-97]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:46-97]()

### Auto factory system and lazy imports

Auto classes provide a common entry point to model families; the test suite, for example, imports `AutoModel` and `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` alongside concrete model classes. Transformers also exposes `_LazyModule` and dependency-availability helpers through its utility package. The Auto mappings and lazy-loading mechanisms are covered in [Auto Classes & Lazy-Loading Factory](#2.2). [tests/test_modeling_common.py:36-45](), [src/transformers/utils/__init__.py:100-112]()

Sources: [tests/test_modeling_common.py:36-45](), [src/transformers/utils/__init__.py:100-112]()

### Model weight loading and conversion

The model utilities import `WeightConverter`, `WeightRenaming`, and `convert_and_load_state_dict_in_model` from `core_model_loading.py`, and obtain model conversion mappings through `conversion_mapping.py`. These components connect checkpoint data to model parameters. For conversion rules and loading paths, see [Model Weight Loading & Conversion](#2.3). [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:49-56]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:49-56]()

### Common modeling layers and utilities

The shared modeling layer includes helpers for RoPE, PyTorch tensor operations, loss mappings, and attention integrations. The common modeling test module also imports `GradientCheckpointingLayer`, showing that shared layer abstractions are exercised across model tests. For details, see [Common Modeling Layers & Utilities](#2.4). [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:78-96](), [tests/test_modeling_common.py:55-63]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:78-96](), [tests/test_modeling_common.py:55-63]()

---

# Page: PreTrainedModel & PreTrainedConfig

# PreTrainedModel & PreTrainedConfig

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the roles of `PreTrainedModel` and `PreTrainedConfig` in the model lifecycle: configuration and checkpoint loading, saving, weight tying, attention implementation choices, gradient checkpointing, and serialization. `src/transformers/modeling_utils.py` imports `PreTrainedConfig` and the core weight-conversion functions; `src/transformers/configuration_utils.py` defines configuration-related utilities and the `SpecificPreTrainedConfigType` type variable [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:46-56]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:59-63]().

**Sources:** [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:46-56](), [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:59-63]()

---

## PreTrainedConfig

`PreTrainedConfig` is the shared configuration abstraction associated with pretrained models. Model-specific configuration classes supply architecture settings; configuration utilities provide shared serialization and compatibility behavior. `src/transformers/modeling_utils.py` imports `PreTrainedConfig`, and configuration utilities define the base-class type variable and layer-type conventions [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:48-50]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:59-90]().

### Serialization and compatibility

The configuration module defines `CONFIG_NAME` as the configuration filename constant used by its utilities, imports `PushToHubMixin` and `cached_file`, and declares special tags for non-finite floating-point values. It also defines allowed attention and MLP layer types, plus a legacy-name mapping and `remap_legacy_layer_types()` for normalizing old layer-type names [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:39-49]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:62-99]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:102-136]().

| Concern | Code entity | Role evidenced by the source |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration filename | `CONFIG_NAME` | Imported by the configuration module for its configuration-file utilities [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:39-47]() |
| Special float values | `_FLOAT_TAG_KEY`, `_FLOAT_TAG_VALUES` | Constants for representing `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:62-63]() |
| Attention-layer vocabulary | `ALLOWED_ATTN_LAYER_TYPES` | Names the supported attention and related layer categories [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:66-82]() |
| Legacy layer names | `_LEGACY_LAYER_TYPE_REMAP` | Maps older names such as `mamba` and `attention` to standardized names [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:93-99]() |
| Layer-type normalization | `remap_legacy_layer_types()` | Returns remapped names for a list, or updates the corresponding configuration attributes when given a config [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:102-136]() |

### Configuration normalization: natural language to code entities

**Diagram: Legacy layer names become standardized configuration values**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["LegacyLayerNames"] --> B["remap_legacy_layer_types"]
    B --> C["_LEGACY_LAYER_TYPE_REMAP"]
    C --> D["StandardizedLayerNames"]
    B --> E["config.layer_types"]
    B --> F["config.mtp_layer_types"]
```

**Sources:** [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:93-136]()

## PreTrainedModel

`PreTrainedModel` is the PyTorch model base abstraction used across the library. `src/transformers/modeling_utils.py` imports PyTorch’s `nn`, the `PreTrainedConfig` type, loading/conversion helpers, and serialization-related utilities [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:35-56]()[src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:98-125]().

`Trainer` imports both `PreTrainedModel` and `unwrap_model`, showing that the base model abstraction is used by training infrastructure as well as loading and serialization utilities [src/transformers/trainer.py:77-78]().

**Sources:** [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:35-56](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:98-125](), [src/transformers/trainer.py:77-78]()

### Loading and saving lifecycle

The loading module imports `cached_file`, checkpoint shard helpers, Safetensors readers and writers, and core conversion functions including `convert_and_load_state_dict_in_model`. It also defines `LoadStateDictConfig`, which groups loading inputs such as a model identifier, Safetensors preference, mismatch handling, sharded metadata, device map, offload folder, and dtype information [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:35-56]()[src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:98-125]()[src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]().

**Diagram: Loading concepts mapped to code entities**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["ModelIdentifierOrPath"] --> B["LoadStateDictConfig"]
    B --> C["cached_file"]
    C --> D["CheckpointShardFiles"]
    D --> E["convert_and_load_state_dict_in_model"]
    F["SafetensorsCheckpoint"] --> G["safe_open"]
    H["SavedWeights"] --> I["safe_save_file"]
```

**Sources:** [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:35-56](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:98-125](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

### Weight conversion and compatibility

`src/transformers/modeling_utils.py` imports `WeightConverter`, `WeightRenaming`, `convert_and_load_state_dict_in_model`, and `revert_weight_conversion` from `core_model_loading.py`, and imports `get_model_conversion_mapping` from `conversion_mapping.py` [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:50-56]().

**Sources:** [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:50-56]()

---

## Weight tying

The model utilities import PyTorch’s `nn`, while modeling tests define example `PreTrainedModel` subclasses with `_tied_weights_keys`. One test fixture maps `"linear_2.weight"` to `"linear.weight"`; another maps multiple target names to the same source [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:41-42]()[tests/utils/test_modeling_utils.py:195-217]().

## Summary

`PreTrainedConfig` supplies shared configuration-related types and utilities, including layer-type compatibility normalization and serialization dependencies. `PreTrainedModel` is the model abstraction used by training code and the central modeling utilities module, which imports checkpoint, conversion, serialization, and attention-backend components [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:39-49]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:59-63]()[src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:102-136]()[src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:35-56]()[src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:76-90]()[src/transformers/trainer.py:77-78]().

# Page: Auto Classes & Lazy-Loading Factory

# Auto Classes & Lazy-Loading Factory

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose & Scope

This page explains how Transformers connects model identifiers and configuration model types to configuration, model, tokenizer, image-processing, and processor implementations. It covers the mapping registries and lazy import mechanisms, plus the interfaces used for optional dependencies and dynamic remote code. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:26-44](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:26-44](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19]()

---

## Architecture Overview

Auto resolution is built from registries that associate model-type keys with class names, and mapping objects that resolve those names to Python classes. `CONFIG_MAPPING_NAMES` is defined in the generated auto mappings module and is used by `configuration_auto.py`; `MODEL_MAPPING_NAMES` and `TOKENIZER_MAPPING_NAMES` provide analogous entries for model and tokenizer classes. [src/transformers/models/auto/auto_mappings.py:21-42](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:23-26](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:21-28](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:37-44](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:59-71]()

For configuration classes, `_LazyConfigMapping.__getitem__` checks registered extra content, looks up the configured class name, converts the model type to a module name, imports that module on demand, and retrieves the class. It falls back to looking up the class at the top-level `transformers` module when it is not found in the model module. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127]()

At the package level, `transformers/__init__.py` documents that `_import_structure` exposes names while deferring their actual imports. The package imports `_LazyModule` and uses it as part of this mechanism; `src/transformers/models/__init__.py` also imports `_LazyModule` and `define_import_structure`. [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:23-40](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-24]()

### Diagram: User-Facing Names to Auto-Mapping Code Entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    User["NaturalLanguageChoice"] --> ModelType["model_type_bert"]
    ModelType --> ConfigNames["CONFIG_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    ConfigNames --> ConfigMapping["CONFIG_MAPPING"]
    ConfigMapping --> LazyConfig["_LazyConfigMapping.__getitem__"]
    LazyConfig --> BertConfig["BertConfig"]

    User --> ModelChoice["NaturalLanguageBaseModel"]
    ModelChoice --> ModelNames["MODEL_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    ModelNames --> AutoMapping["_LazyAutoMapping"]
    AutoMapping --> BertModel["BertModel"]

    User --> TokenizerChoice["NaturalLanguageTokenizer"]
    TokenizerChoice --> TokenizerNames["TOKENIZER_MAPPING_NAMES"]
    TokenizerNames --> TokenizerClass["BertTokenizer"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/auto_mappings.py:24-35](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:161-161](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:21-28](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:41-50](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:37-44](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:63-79]()

### Diagram: Package-Level Lazy Import Bridge

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    User["NaturalLanguageImport"] --> PublicName["transformers.AutoModel"]
    PublicName --> ImportStructure["_import_structure"]
    ImportStructure --> LazyProxy["_LazyModule"]
    LazyProxy --> ModuleName["transformers.models.auto"]
    ModuleName --> Factory["AutoModel"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:23-40](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-24]()

---

# Core Components

## 1. Lazy Mappings: `_LazyConfigMapping` and `_LazyAutoMapping`

`_LazyConfigMapping` is an `OrderedDict` subclass that keeps the string-to-class-name registry separately from module and extra-content caches. Its `__getitem__` resolves a key by checking `_extra_content`, retrieving the mapped class name, converting the key with `model_type_to_module_name`, importing the model module if it has not already been cached, and retrieving the named class. If the class is not in that module, it checks the top-level `transformers` module. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127]()

`CONFIG_MAPPING` is an instance of `_LazyConfigMapping` initialized from `CONFIG_MAPPING_NAMES`. The mapping supports runtime registration through `register`; registrations are stored in `_extra_content`, and duplicate built-in keys raise a `ValueError` unless `exist_ok` is true. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:143-161]()

`_LazyAutoMapping` is imported by `modeling_auto.py`, `tokenization_auto.py`, and `image_processing_auto.py` as the mapping abstraction used by their auto-class registries. Its implementation is in `auto_factory.py`; the supplied file contents do not include that implementation, so details of its lookup and caching behavior are not specified here. [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:21-28](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:35-44](), [src/transformers/models/auto/image_processing_auto.py:38-45]()

Model-type normalization is handled by `model_type_to_module_name`: special keys are translated through `SPECIAL_MODEL_TYPE_TO_MODULE_NAME`, while other keys replace hyphens with underscores. `config_class_to_model_type` performs the reverse registry search for a configuration class name, including registered extra content. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:54-65](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:72-98]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:54-65](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:72-98](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:143-161](), [src/transformers/models/auto/modeling_auto.py:21-28](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:35-44](), [src/transformers/models/auto/image_processing_auto.py:38-45]()

## 2. The `_LazyModule` Import Proxy

The package initializer states that `_import_structure` maps submodules to exported object names and defers actual imports until those objects are requested. It imports `_LazyModule` from `transformers.utils`; the supplied excerpt does not include `_LazyModule`’s implementation, so its attribute-resolution internals are not detailed here. [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:30-40]()

The top-level import structure includes entries for configuration, tokenization, processing, pipelines, and other package areas. The `models` package likewise imports `_LazyModule` and `define_import_structure`; its `TYPE_CHECKING` branch lists model modules for static typing. [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-87](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:150-170](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-38]()

This package-level laziness is distinct from mapping-level laziness: `_LazyModule` concerns deferred package exports, while `_LazyConfigMapping` resolves a model-type key to a configuration class by importing the corresponding model module. [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127]()

Sources: [src/transformers/__init__.py:15-19](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:30-40](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:61-87](), [src/transformers/__init__.py:150-170](), [src/transformers/models/__init__.py:20-38](), [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:101-127]()

## 3. Dummy Objects for Optional Backends

`dummy_pt_objects.py` defines placeholder classes using `DummyObject` as their metaclass. For example, `Cache` and `DynamicCache` declare `torch` as a required backend and call `requires_backends` from their constructors. These placeholders allow the package to expose names while reporting a backend requirement when construction is attempted. [src/transformers/utils/dummy_pt_objects.py:1-16]()

The same pattern is used for other PyTorch-facing names in the file, including `EncoderDecoderCache`, `QuantizedCache`, and `StaticCache`. [src/transformers/utils/dummy_pt_objects.py:19-38]()

Sources: [src/transformers/utils/dummy_pt_objects.py:1-16](), [src/transformers/utils/dummy_pt_objects.py:19-38]()

---

# Dynamic Module System for Trusted Remote Code

The Auto Config and Auto Tokenizer modules import `get_class_from_dynamic_module` and `resolve_trust_remote_code` from `dynamic_module_utils`. This establishes the dynamic-code resolution interface used by those factories. The supplied contents do not include the implementations or call sites in those modules, so this page does not infer the precise download, validation, caching, or execution sequence. [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:23-25](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:26-28]()

### Diagram: Dynamic-Code Interface Boundaries

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    AutoConfig["configuration_auto.py"] --> TrustResolver["resolve_trust_remote_code"]
    AutoConfig --> ClassLoader["get_class_from_dynamic_module"]
    AutoTokenizer["tokenization_auto.py"] --> TrustResolver
    AutoTokenizer --> ClassLoader
    TrustResolver --> DynamicUtils["dynamic_module_utils.py"]
    ClassLoader --> DynamicUtils
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/auto/configuration_auto.py:23-25](), [src/transformers/models/auto/tokenization_auto.py:26-28]()

# Specialization of Auto Classes & Their Registries

The registries associate model-type or configuration-name keys with class names. The table below identifies the mappings shown in the supplied source excerpts; it does not enumerate every auto class or its complete mapping. # Repository Consistency Checks

`utils/check_repo.py` documents checks for model registration in package initializers and auto classes, as well as checks that auto mappings are correctly defined and importable. It imports the configuration, feature-extractor, image-processor, processor, and tokenizer mapping names and uses `get_values` from `auto_factory.py`. [utils/check_repo.py:14-22](), [utils/check_repo.py:43-51]()

The generated `auto_mappings.py` header directs contributors to update model configuration `model_type` definitions and regenerate mappings with `utils/check_auto.py --fix_and_overwrite`, rather than editing the generated mapping file manually. [src/transformers/models/auto/auto_mappings.py:1-5]()

# Page: Model Weight Loading & Conversion

# Model Weight Loading & Conversion

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the checkpoint-conversion layer in Transformers: how conversion rules associate checkpoint names with model parameter names, how `ConversionOps` represents tensor transformations, and how the mapping registry relates model families to shared conversion patterns. The implementation is centered on `core_model_loading.py` and `conversion_mapping.py`. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:14-46](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:15-35]()

The page focuses on conversion mechanics and mapping data. It does not assume a specific end-to-end call sequence from `PreTrainedModel.from_pretrained()`: the available source excerpts define conversion primitives and mapping construction, but do not show the loader’s full orchestration path. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:14-46](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179]()

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:14-46](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:15-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179]()

---

## System architecture and data flow

`core_model_loading.py` defines the conversion operations and matching support; `conversion_mapping.py` imports those types and uses them to build checkpoint conversion mappings. The mapping module also declares `_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN`, which associates model identifiers with shared conversion patterns—for example, several MoE model identifiers map to `qwen2_moe`, while `minimax` identifiers map to `mixtral`. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73]()

The diagram shows the relationship between checkpoint naming, mapping declarations, and conversion primitives. It does not imply a particular loader call sequence. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73]()

### Diagram: Mapping declarations and conversion entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ModelIdentifier["model_identifier"] --> PatternLookup["_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN"]
    PatternLookup --> ConversionPattern["shared_conversion_pattern"]
    MappingBuilder["_build_checkpoint_conversion_mapping"] --> Rules["WeightRenaming and conversion rules"]
    Rules --> CoreTypes["WeightConverter and ConversionOps"]
    CoreTypes --> GlobMatcher["build_glob_alternation"]
    CheckpointNames["checkpoint_names"] --> GlobMatcher
```

Sources: [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-98]()

### Natural-language concepts to code entities

| Concept | Code entity | Role |
|---|---|---|
| A rule for translating checkpoint keys | `WeightRenaming` | Imported by the mapping module and included in mapping declarations. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35]() |
| A rule that combines name and tensor conversion | `WeightConverter` | Imported by the mapping module; `build_glob_alternation` treats it alongside `WeightRenaming` when building matching patterns. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]() |
| A tensor transformation | `ConversionOps` | Abstract base class defining `convert` and `reverse_op`. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:81-99]() |
| A pattern lookup by model identifier | `_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN` | Associates model names with shared conversion-pattern names. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73]() |
| Mapping-rule construction | `_build_checkpoint_conversion_mapping` | Starts constructing conversion rules using `WeightRenaming` instances. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179]() |
| A combined matcher for patterns | `build_glob_alternation` | Builds a regex alternation and maps its named groups to source and target patterns. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]() |

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-99](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179]()

---

## Conversion operations and tensor transformations

`ConversionOps` is an abstract base for weight-conversion operations. Its interface requires a `convert` method and exposes a `reverse_op` property; concrete operations can therefore describe both a forward conversion and a corresponding reverse operation where implemented. The available excerpt shows `_IdentityOp`, `Chunk`, and `Split`. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:81-99](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:101-180]()

| Operation | Behavior shown in the implementation |
|---|---|
| `_IdentityOp` | Returns its input dictionary unchanged. Its docstring describes it as a pass-through reverse operation for dequantized weights. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:101-110]() |
| `Chunk` | Splits a single input tensor into equally sized chunks along `dim`; it uses the target-pattern count to determine the number of chunks. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:112-131]() |
| `Chunk.get_target_patterns` | If `num_shards_attribute` is set, reads that attribute from the text config and expands a wildcard in the target pattern into numbered targets. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:133-143]() |
| `Chunk.reverse_op` | Returns `Concatenate` configured with the same dimension and shard attribute. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:145-147]() |
| `Split` | Splits a single input tensor according to target parameter sizes obtained from the model, along the configured dimension. The implementation warns that this operation is not TP-safe for sharded fused tensors. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-176]() |
| `Split.reverse_op` | Returns `Concatenate` configured with the same dimension. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:178-180]() |

`Chunk.convert` and `Split.convert` reject an input dictionary containing more than one key. Both accept a tensor or a list of tensors as the value for the single key and use the first list element when the value is a list. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:120-131](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:157-176]()

### Diagram: `Chunk` and `Split` behavior

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["single_input_tensor"] --> Operation{"Conversion_Operation"}
    Operation -->|"Chunk"| TargetCount["target_count_or_config_shard_count"]
    TargetCount --> EqualPieces["equal_sized_chunks_along_dim"]
    EqualPieces --> ChunkTargets["target_patterns"]
    Operation -->|"Split"| ModelParams["model_target_parameter_shapes"]
    ModelParams --> SizedPieces["pieces_sized_to_target_parameters"]
    SizedPieces --> SplitTargets["target_patterns"]
    ChunkTargets --> Reverse["Concatenate_reverse_operation"]
    SplitTargets --> Reverse
```

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:112-147](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-180]()

### Pattern matching

`build_glob_alternation` accepts `WeightRenaming`, `WeightConverter`, or string patterns. For renaming and converter objects it creates a named regex group for each source pattern; for a string it creates a group for that string. A `*` in a pattern is converted to `.*`. The function returns the compiled alternation together with mappings from group names to source and target patterns. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]()

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:81-99](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:101-180]()

---

## Core classes and mapping workflow

### `WeightRenaming` and `WeightConverter`

`conversion_mapping.py` imports `WeightRenaming` and `WeightConverter` from `core_model_loading.py`, alongside the conversion-operation classes used in mapping rules. `build_glob_alternation` handles `WeightRenaming` and `WeightConverter` through their `source_patterns` and `target_patterns` attributes, associating source-pattern groups with the first target pattern. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]()

The excerpt establishes the types’ use in pattern matching, but does not include the definitions of `WeightRenaming` or `WeightConverter` themselves. Their internal conversion order and full constructor/API details are therefore not specified here. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]()

### Diagram: Pattern matching entities

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class WeightRenaming {
        "source_patterns"
        "target_patterns"
    }
    class WeightConverter {
        "source_patterns"
        "target_patterns"
    }
    class ConversionOps {
        "<<abstract>>"
        "convert"
        "reverse_op"
    }
    class Chunk {
        "convert"
        "get_target_patterns"
        "reverse_op"
    }
    class Split {
        "convert"
        "reverse_op"
    }
    WeightConverter --> ConversionOps : "uses conversion operations"
    ConversionOps <|-- Chunk
    ConversionOps <|-- Split
    WeightRenaming ..> WeightConverter : "shared pattern interface used by matcher"
```

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:81-99](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:112-180]()

### `_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN`

`_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN` groups model identifiers under shared pattern names. The shown entries include `minimax` and `minimax_m2` mapped to `mixtral`; a broad set of MoE identifiers—including `afmoe`, `deepseek_v2`, `deepseek_v3`, `qwen3_moe`, and `cohere2_moe`—mapped to `qwen2_moe;` and vision, multimodal, and audio model identifiers mapped to patterns such as `CLIPVisionModel`, `LlavaModel`, and `Qwen2AudioModel`. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-110]()

The mapping also includes class-name keys, such as `AriaModel` and `PaliGemmaModel` mapping to `LlavaModel`, and ViT-style vision classes mapping to `ViTModel`. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:112-151]()

### `_build_checkpoint_conversion_mapping`

`_build_checkpoint_conversion_mapping` begins a dictionary of named checkpoint conversion rules. In the shown `hy_v4` entry, `WeightRenaming` rules translate checkpoint key fragments such as `.learnable_sink_param` and `.linear_gate`, and map hierarchical-connections names to alternative target fragments. The shown `cosmos3_edge` entry begins by prefixing embedding, normalization, and layer keys with `model.language_model`. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179]()

Sources: [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-73](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:74-110](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:112-151](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:154-179](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:49-78]()
