## Specialized conversion patterns

### Fused QKV weights

`Chunk` provides an operation for splitting one tensor into equally sized pieces, while `Split` provides an operation for splitting one tensor according to the target model parameters’ sizes. These operations can represent different split requirements for a fused tensor, but the available excerpts do not show a specific QKV mapping declaration or establish which operation is used for a particular model’s Q, K, and V projections. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:112-131](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-176]()

`Split` explicitly warns that it is not TP-safe for a sharded fused tensor: it derives split sizes from the target parameters on the model, whereas a sharded fused tensor requires each target’s local slice. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-176]()

### MoE expert stacking

The conversion module imports `MergeModulelist` and includes shared MoE conversion-pattern identifiers such as `mixtral` and `qwen2_moe`. This establishes that module-list conversion is part of the available mapping vocabulary and that multiple MoE model identifiers share named conversion patterns. The available excerpts do not show `MergeModulelist`’s implementation or a particular expert-stacking rule, so they do not establish its tensor layout or resulting shape. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-71]()

### RoPE permutations

The conversion module imports `PermuteForRope` as a conversion operation available to mapping declarations. The available excerpt does not include that operation’s implementation or a specific mapping that invokes it; consequently, the precise permutation and the checkpoint conventions it handles cannot be derived from these lines. [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35]()

### Diagram: Specialized conversion vocabulary

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    FusedTensor["fused_tensor"] --> Chunk["Chunk"]
    FusedTensor --> Split["Split"]
    Chunk --> EqualTargetPieces["equal_sized_target_pieces"]
    Split --> ParameterSizedPieces["target_parameter_sized_pieces"]
    MoePattern["moe_model_identifier"] --> SharedPattern["_MODEL_TO_CONVERSION_PATTERN"]
    SharedPattern --> MergeModulelist["MergeModulelist"]
    RopeMapping["rope_conversion_mapping"] --> PermuteForRope["PermuteForRope"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:112-147](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-176](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:21-35](), [src/transformers/conversion_mapping.py:43-71]()

---

## Loading, sharding, and integration boundaries

`core_model_loading.py` imports distributed sharding helpers, device/offload helpers, and the loading-report type alongside the conversion primitives. These imports show the module’s integration boundaries, but the available excerpt does not show how those helpers are invoked in the loading path. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:31-38]()

The `Chunk` implementation can derive a number of target shards from a config attribute, using `config.get_text_config()` to read the configured attribute. `Split`, by contrast, obtains each target’s split size from the corresponding model parameter. Its docstring specifically cautions against using it for TP-sharded fused tensors. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:133-143](), [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:150-176]()

# Page: Common Modeling Layers & Utilities

# Common Modeling Layers & Utilities

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This section describes shared PyTorch modeling infrastructure: activation checkpointing and reusable layers in `modeling_layers.py`, attention-mask composition in `masking_utils.py`, RoPE parameter initialization and runtime updates in `modeling_rope_utils.py`, foundational helpers in `pytorch_utils.py`, and task-loss helpers in `loss/`. These components provide common behavior for model implementations rather than defining a particular architecture. 

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_layers.py:54-164](), [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:44-179](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:34-151](), [src/transformers/pytorch_utils.py:50-179](), [src/transformers/loss/loss_utils.py:32-166]()

---

## Gradient Checkpointing Infrastructure

### Overview

`GradientCheckpointingLayer` is a `torch.nn.Module` base class that intercepts calls to a layer and routes them through the configured checkpoint function when gradient checkpointing is enabled during training. Checkpointing reduces activation memory by recomputing intermediate values during backward propagation. 

When checkpointing is active, the layer adjusts cache-related keyword arguments before invoking the checkpoint function. This avoids retaining or reusing cache state in a recomputed forward pass. Otherwise, the layer follows the ordinary module call path. 

### Call Behavior

| Condition or operation | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Checkpointing is not enabled, or the module is not training | Calls the normal `torch.nn.Module` path. |
| Checkpointing is enabled during training | Disables applicable caching arguments, then calls `_gradient_checkpointing_func`. |
| Cache arguments are changed | Emits a warning once to make the adjustment visible. |
| Inputs need to participate in checkpointed gradient computation | Passes them as positional arguments; keyword-only inputs can cause issues with reentrant checkpointing. |

The checkpoint function receives the underlying module call with adjusted keyword arguments and the original positional arguments. This preserves the layer’s normal forward implementation while changing how its activations are retained. 

### Diagram: `GradientCheckpointingLayer` Call Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["GradientCheckpointingLayer.__call__"] --> B{"gradient_checkpointing and training"}
    B -->|"No"| C["Normal module call"]
    B -->|"Yes"| D["Adjust cache-related kwargs"]
    D --> E["Warn when applicable"]
    E --> F["_gradient_checkpointing_func"]
    F --> G["Layer output"]
    C --> G
```

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_layers.py:54-112]()

---

## Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) Utilities

### Overview

`modeling_rope_utils.py` provides RoPE parameter initialization and runtime frequency updates. Its initialization functions compute inverse frequencies and scaling values from model configuration, while `dynamic_rope_update` wraps a RoPE forward method to update frequencies when the configured RoPE type requires it. 

RoPE configuration is also integrated with `PreTrainedConfig` through `RotaryEmbeddingConfigMixin`. 

### Dynamic Updates

The `dynamic_rope_update` decorator selects update behavior based on `rope_type` and then calls the wrapped RoPE forward method. For dynamic RoPE, `dynamic_frequency_update` recomputes `inv_freq` when the sequence grows beyond the cached range and restores the original frequencies when the sequence returns to the original scale. 

For `longrope`, `longrope_frequency_update` selects between long- and short-context inverse-frequency tensors based on the maximum position ID. If the long-frequency tensor has not yet been initialized, it derives it through the initializer associated with the configured RoPE type. 

### Initialization and Update Responsibilities

| Entity | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS` | Associates RoPE types with initializer functions used to compute parameters. |
| `_compute_linear_scaling_rope_parameters` | Computes inverse frequencies for linear scaling. |
| `dynamic_rope_update` | Wraps a RoPE forward method and dispatches dynamic or LongRoPE updates when needed. |
| `dynamic_frequency_update` | Handles dynamic-frequency growth and reset behavior. |
| `longrope_frequency_update` | Selects the appropriate short- or long-context frequency values. |

### Diagram: RoPE Configuration to Forward Update

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["PreTrainedConfig.rope_parameters"] --> B["ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS"]
    B --> C["RoPE inverse frequencies"]
    D["RoPE forward(x, position_ids)"] --> E["dynamic_rope_update"]
    E --> F{"rope_type"}
    F -->|"dynamic"| G["dynamic_frequency_update"]
    F -->|"longrope"| H["longrope_frequency_update"]
    F -->|"Other"| I["Use current frequencies"]
    G --> J["Wrapped RoPE forward"]
    H --> J
    I --> J
```

Sources: [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:34-38](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:34-130](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:133-151]()

---

## Shared Modeling Layers in `modeling_layers.py`

`modeling_layers.py` contains reusable model components. In addition to `GradientCheckpointingLayer`, it defines `GenericForSequenceClassification`, a generic classification wrapper that constructs a base model from configuration and applies a classification head to its hidden states. 

### `GenericForSequenceClassification`

`GenericForSequenceClassification` creates its base model using `AutoModel.from_config(config)` and adds a linear scoring layer. Its forward path passes inputs through the base model, applies the classifier, and returns `SequenceClassifierOutputWithPast`. 

The wrapper separates the generic classification task head from the selected base architecture: the configuration determines which model is instantiated, while the class supplies the classification-oriented structure. 

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_layers.py:54-164]()

---

## Attention Masking Utilities (`masking_utils.py`)

### Mask Functions and Composition

`masking_utils.py` represents attention visibility with callable mask functions. These functions take batch, head, query, and key/value indices; mask combinators then compose them into more complex visibility rules. 

- `and_masks` returns a function that intersects its input masks.
- `or_masks` returns a function that unions its input masks.
- `causal_mask_function` permits key/value positions at or before the query position.
- `bidirectional_mask_function` provides a full bidirectional pattern.
- `padding_mask_function` derives visibility from a two-dimensional padding mask.

### Attention-Pattern Overlays

Overlay functions add structural constraints that can be combined with causal or bidirectional masks. `sliding_window_overlay` restricts visibility by a query-relative window; `chunked_overlay` restricts attention to the same chunk; and `blockwise_overlay` enables bidirectional attention within a non-text block. 

The module also supplies composed helpers, including `sliding_window_causal_mask_function`, `sliding_window_bidirectional_mask_function`, and `chunked_causal_mask_function`. These are built by combining overlays with base causal or bidirectional functions. 

| Masking primitive | Pattern |
|---|---|
| `causal_mask_function` | Query positions can attend to the current and preceding key/value positions. |
| `sliding_window_causal_mask_function` | Causal visibility constrained by a sliding window. |
| `chunked_causal_mask_function` | Causal visibility constrained to a chunk, accounting for left padding. |
| `blockwise_overlay` | Allows bidirectional attention within a shared non-text block. |
| `padding_mask_function` | Uses the padding tensor to determine key/value visibility. |

Sources: [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:44-175]()

### Diagram: Composing an Attention Pattern

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Base mask function"] --> C["and_masks"]
    B["Pattern overlay"] --> C
    C --> D["Combined mask function"]
    D --> E["Attention visibility"]
    A --> F["causal_mask_function"]
    B --> G["sliding_window_overlay"]
    B --> H["chunked_overlay"]
    B --> I["blockwise_overlay"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:44-69](), [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:72-127](), [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:130-161]()

---

## PyTorch Utilities (`pytorch_utils.py`)

`pytorch_utils.py` provides shared PyTorch operations and compatibility helpers used by model implementations. The module includes layer transformations, a GPT-style linear layer, chunked forward execution, and a wrapper around PyTorch’s internal softmax backward operation. 

### Key Components

- **`softmax_backward_data`** calls PyTorch’s `_softmax_backward_data` with the dimension and dtype taken from the parent operation’s output.
- **`prune_linear_layer`** selects weights and, where applicable, bias entries along a requested dimension to produce a new `nn.Linear`. It is documented for uses such as removing attention heads.
- **`Conv1D`** implements the GPT-style projection with weights stored transposed relative to `nn.Linear`; its forward pass applies a matrix operation and restores the output shape.
- **`apply_chunking_to_forward`** divides inputs into chunks along a selected dimension, applies a forward function to each chunk, and is intended for functions independent across that dimension. It checks the number of input tensors and their chunk dimensions.

Sources: [src/transformers/pytorch_utils.py:50-179]()

---

## Loss Helpers (`loss/` Subpackage)

The `loss/` subpackage contains shared loss functions used by model task heads. The `loss_utils.py` helpers cover cross-entropy normalization and common causal language modeling, masked language modeling, and sequence classification loss paths. 

### `loss_utils.py` Functions

| Function | Role |
|---|---|
| `fixed_cross_entropy` | Computes cross entropy with support for `num_items_in_batch` normalization and a selected reduction. |
| `ForCausalLMLoss` | Prepares causal language modeling labels, including shifting for next-token prediction, and computes the loss. |
| `ForMaskedLMLoss` | Computes masked language modeling loss over token predictions. |
| `ForSequenceClassificationLoss` | Selects loss behavior for regression, single-label classification, or multi-label classification. |

These helpers centralize recurring task-loss behavior so model heads can use common loss implementations rather than independently defining the same task logic. 

Sources: [src/transformers/loss/loss_utils.py:32-166]()

---

## Natural-Language Concepts and Code Entities

This map connects the modeling concerns discussed on this page to the symbols that implement them, bridging natural language space to code entity space.

### Diagram: Shared Modeling Concepts to Implementation Symbols

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Activation checkpointing"] --> B["GradientCheckpointingLayer"]
    B --> C["modeling_layers.py"]
    D["Generic sequence classification"] --> E["GenericForSequenceClassification"]
    E --> C
    F["Attention visibility"] --> G["and_masks"]
    F --> H["causal_mask_function"]
    F --> I["sliding_window_overlay"]
    G --> J["masking_utils.py"]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    K["Rotary position scaling"] --> L["dynamic_rope_update"]
    L --> M["dynamic_frequency_update"]
    L --> N["longrope_frequency_update"]
    M --> O["modeling_rope_utils.py"]
    N --> O
    P["Layer and tensor helpers"] --> Q["Conv1D"]
    P --> R["prune_linear_layer"]
    P --> S["apply_chunking_to_forward"]
    Q --> T["pytorch_utils.py"]
    R --> T
    S --> T
    U["Task losses"] --> V["ForCausalLMLoss"]
    U --> W["ForMaskedLMLoss"]
    U --> X["ForSequenceClassificationLoss"]
    V --> Y["loss/loss_utils.py"]
    W --> Y
    X --> Y
```

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_layers.py:54-164](), [src/transformers/masking_utils.py:44-175](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:34-151](), [src/transformers/pytorch_utils.py:50-179](), [src/transformers/loss/loss_utils.py:32-166]()

---

## Data Flow: RoPE Initialization and Forward Update

Configuration supplies RoPE parameters; initialization functions produce frequency values, and the decorated forward path refreshes those values for dynamic or LongRoPE configurations before calling the underlying implementation.

### Diagram: RoPE Parameter and Forward Data Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Config as "PreTrainedConfig"
    participant Init as "ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS"
    participant Decorator as "dynamic_rope_update"
    participant Update as "dynamic_frequency_update or longrope_frequency_update"
    participant Forward as "Wrapped RoPE forward"

    Config->>Init: "Provide RoPE configuration"
    Init->>Init: "Compute inverse frequencies and scaling"
    Decorator->>Update: "Dispatch according to rope_type"
    Update->>Update: "Refresh inv_freq when required"
    Update->>Forward: "Continue with updated frequency state"
    Forward->>Forward: "Compute RoPE outputs"
```

Sources: [src/transformers/configuration_utils.py:34-38](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:34-130](), [src/transformers/modeling_rope_utils.py:133-151]()

# Page: Type Checking & Static Analysis

# Type Checking & Static Analysis

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md](.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md)
- [Makefile](Makefile)

</details>



This page covers the static analysis and type-checking infrastructure used in the Hugging Face Transformers codebase. It details the `ty`-based type-checking workflow, how typing commands are structured in the build system, and advanced typing patterns such as `src/transformers/_typing.py` protocols, `TypeGuard` functions for dynamic device backends, method overloads, generic containers with defaults, and union narrowing rules.

Sources: `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:1-156]()`, `[Makefile:1-101]()`

---

## 1. The `ty`-Based Type Checking Workflow

Static analysis in Transformers relies on the `ty` type checker combined with repository-specific structure checkers. The primary entry point for developers and CI pipelines is defined in the root `Makefile` [Makefile:1-101]().

The typing check suite is executed via the `typing` target, which runs `utils/checkers.py` with the `TYPING_CHECKERS` list (consisting of `types` and `modeling_structure`) [Makefile:14-15, 46-48]().

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Make Command: make typing"] --> B["Makefile:typing target"]
    B --> C["Checker Script: utils/checkers.py"]
    C --> D["Typing Checkers: TYPING_CHECKERS"]
    D --> E["Types Check: types"]
    D --> F["Model Structure: modeling_structure"]
```
*Figure 1: Natural Language Space to Code Entity Space mapping for the typing workflow.*

Sources: `[Makefile:13-16, 46-48]()`, `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:15-21]()`

### Local Execution and Fine-Grained Targeting

When investigating typing errors locally or fixing issues flagged by CI, developers run `ty check` directly with specific exclusion flags to bypass protobuf or generated artifacts [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:23-26]():

```bash
ty check --respect-ignore-files --exclude '**/*_pb*' <target>
```

Sources: `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:23-26]()`

---

## 2. Protocols, `TypeGuards`, and Dynamic Attributes

To handle optional third-party hardware modules (such as `torch.npu`, `torch.xpu`, or `torch.compiler`), Transformers implements custom type guards and protocols inside `src/transformers/_typing.py` [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:136-156]().

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Dynamic Module Check"] --> B["src/transformers/_typing.py"]
    B --> C["TypeGuard Function: has_torch_npu"]
    C --> D["Type Narrowing: TypeGuard[Any]"]
    B --> E["Mixin Self-Types: self: ProtocolType"]
```
*Figure 2: Code Entity Space mapping for `_typing.py` type guards and mixin protocols.*

### TypeGuards for Device Backends

Instead of raw `getattr()` or `hasattr()` calls that confuse static analyzers, type guards are defined in `src/transformers/_typing.py` [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:141-152]():

```python
def has_torch_npu(mod: ModuleType) -> TypeGuard[Any]:
    return hasattr(mod, "npu") and mod.npu.is_available()
```

When called directly within an `if` condition, `ty` narrows the module type, permitting safe attribute access without explicit casts [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:146-151]().

Sources: `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:136-156]()`

---

## 3. Advanced Typing Patterns: Overloads, Generics, and Union Narrowing

To ensure robust static analysis without littering the codebase with `# type: ignore` comments, Transformers relies on several advanced typing patterns:

* **Union Narrowing**: Use `isinstance()`, `if x is None: raise`, and `hasattr()` to narrow types [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:38-57](). Never use `assert` for control-flow narrowing where runtime validation is required.
* **Local Variables for Closures**: Copy nullable instance attributes (e.g., `self.batching_manager`) to local variables before narrowing, because static analyzers cannot track mutations or non-nil states across closure boundaries [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:59-68]().
* **Chained Call Splitting**: Split complex method chains (e.g., `func().method()`) when intermediate return types are broad unions, allowing explicit checks on intermediate variables [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:71-81]().
* **Method Overloads**: Use `@overload` for methods exhibiting input-dependent return types (such as `__getitem__` with different key types) to eliminate usage-site `cast()` calls [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:91-110]().
* **Generic Containers with Defaults**: Parameterize container classes using `Generic[_V]` where `_V = TypeVar("_V", default=Any)` (imported from `typing_extensions`), ensuring unparameterized usages default to `Any` while allowing methods like `.to()` to return narrowed container types [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:112-135]().

Sources: `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:36-135]()`

---

## 4. Suppression Policy and Error Triage

When addressing typing failures in local runs or CI logs, engineers triage errors using a structured priority list:

1. **Fix incorrect type hints at source**: Ensure parameter annotations accurately reflect permissible runtime values [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:83-84]().
2. **Annotate untyped attributes**: Explicitly type instance variables initialized in `__init__` or class-level attributes set dynamically [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:86-90]().
3. **Use protocols and TypeGuards**: Resolve mixin self-type dependencies and dynamic module attribute accesses [non-source/impl context and .ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:136-156]().

Sources: `[.ai/skills/add-or-fix-type-checking/SKILL.md:28-156]()`

---

## Purpose and Scope

This page surveys the main model-family categories in `transformers/models/` and links to child pages for implementation details. The examples below illustrate how model-specific components—such as normalization, rotary embeddings, attention, and MLPs—appear in code; they are not a complete inventory of the repository. [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-66]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-66]()

---

### Architectural Taxonomy

Model families can be grouped by sequence architecture and modality. Within the provided implementations, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, and Qwen2 expose decoder-model components, while Mixtral and Qwen2-MoE include explicit expert-routing components. The family pages cover additional architectures and variants. [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-66]()[src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47]()[src/transformers/models/mixtral/modeling_mixtral.py:55-129]()[src/transformers/models/qwen2_moe/modeling_qwen2_moe.py:54-69]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-66](), [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47](), [src/transformers/models/mixtral/modeling_mixtral.py:55-129](), [src/transformers/models/qwen2_moe/modeling_qwen2_moe.py:54-69]()

---

#### 3.1 Decoder-Only Language Models (LLMs)

Decoder-only models form the autoregressive language-modeling family. The available implementations show recurring components across model-specific files: Llama defines `LlamaRMSNorm` and `LlamaRotaryEmbedding`; Mistral defines `MistralMLP` and `apply_rotary_pos_emb`; Gemma defines `GemmaRMSNorm` and `GemmaMLP`; Qwen2 defines `Qwen2MLP` and `Qwen2RotaryEmbedding`. [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-116]()[src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-80]()[src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-97]()[src/transformers/models/qwen2/modeling_qwen2.py:34-94]()

The child page covers Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen2/3, Phi, Cohere, StableLM, Starcoder2, OLMo, Falcon, GPT-2, GPT-NeoX, and shared components such as RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA, and SwiGLU. For details, see [Decoder-Only Language Models (LLMs)](#3.1).

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-116](), [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-92](), [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-97](), [src/transformers/models/qwen2/modeling_qwen2.py:34-94]()

---

#### 3.2 Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Models

MoE implementations add routing and expert components to model architectures. In Mixtral, `MixtralTopKRouter` selects experts and `MixtralSparseMoeBlock` passes token states and routing outputs to `MixtralExperts`. [src/transformers/models/mixtral/modeling_mixtral.py:55-129]() Qwen2-MoE also provides a model-specific normalization layer, `Qwen2MoeRMSNorm`. [src/transformers/models/qwen2_moe/modeling_qwen2_moe.py:54-69]()

The child page surveys Mixtral, Qwen MoE, DeepSeek, GPT-OSS, Llama4, DBRX, and other MoE families, including routing, expert stacking, auxiliary loss, and expert parallelism. For details, see [Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Models](#3.2).

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mixtral/modeling_mixtral.py:55-129](), [src/transformers/models/qwen2_moe/modeling_qwen2_moe.py:54-69]()

---

#### 3.3 State Space & Hybrid Models

State-space and hybrid families provide alternatives to architectures built solely from attention layers. The child page covers Mamba, Mamba2, Jamba, Bamba, FalconMamba/H1, Zamba, GraniteMoEHybrid, NemotronH, Qwen3-Next, LFM2, xLSTM, and RWKV, focusing on recurrence and hybrid layer patterns.

For details, see [State Space & Hybrid Models](#3.3).

# Page: Decoder-Only Language Models (LLMs)

# Decoder-Only Language Models (LLMs)

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page describes the decoder-only language-model implementations represented in the codebase, with emphasis on shared decoder components (such as RMS normalization, Rotary Positional Embeddings, Grouped-Query Attention, and SwiGLU MLPs) as well as concrete implementations like Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Gemma 2, and Gemma 3 [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:19-45](). The architecture survey also encompasses Qwen2/3, Phi, Cohere, StableLM, Starcoder2, OLMo, Falcon, GPT-2, and GPT-NeoX families.

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:19-45]()

---

## Core Architecture Pattern

A decoder-only causal language model maps token IDs to hidden states, processes those states through consecutive decoder layers containing self-attention and feed-forward networks, and produces vocabulary logits for next-token prediction.

The codebase reuses several design elements across these models:
- **Token Embeddings:** Scaling or standard embedding lookups mapping discrete token IDs to continuous representations [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:49-60]().
- **Attention and Positional Encoding:** RoPE-based rotary embeddings applied to query and key tensors [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-149]().
- **Gated MLPs (SwiGLU):** Multi-projection feed-forward networks (`gate_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`) with elementwise gating [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47]().
- **Normalization:** RMS normalization layers applied prior to attention and feed-forward operations [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-69]().

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:21-45](), [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:49-96]()

---

## Data Flow and Entity Mapping in Llama

The diagram below maps common decoder concepts to specific code symbols in the Llama implementation (`src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py`).

### Diagram: Llama shared components and data relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["input_ids"] --> Embeddings["model embedding stage"]
    Embeddings --> Hidden["hidden states"]
    Hidden --> Norm["LlamaRMSNorm"]
    Hidden --> Position["position_ids"]
    Position --> Rotary["LlamaRotaryEmbedding"]
    Rotary --> CosSin["cos and sin"]
    Hidden --> QK["query and key tensors"]
    CosSin --> Apply["apply_rotary_pos_emb"]
    QK --> Apply
    Apply --> Rotated["rotated query and key"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-69](), [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-116](), [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:126-149]()

### Component Notes

- `LlamaRMSNorm.forward`: Records input dtype, converts hidden states to `float32`, computes mean squared magnitude across the final dimension, scales by the reciprocal square root plus epsilon, and casts back before applying the learned weight [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-66]().
- `LlamaRotaryEmbedding`: Selects a RoPE initialization function based on configuration, deriving inverse frequencies from `rope_theta` and head dimensions. Its `forward` pass uses `position_ids` to produce cosine and sine tensors [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-116]().
- `apply_rotary_pos_emb`: Broadcasts cosine and sine tensors, combining each query/key tensor with its half-rotated form computed by `rotate_half` [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:119-149]().

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-149]()

---

## Shared Components and Implementation Details

### Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)

Position-dependent cosine and sine values are computed and applied directly to query and key tensors. In Llama, Gemma, and Gemma 2, rotary embedding classes store inverse frequencies and derive sinusoidal bounds from `position_ids` [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-116](). The helper `apply_rotary_pos_emb` handles broadcasting and tensor rotation [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:119-149]().

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-149](), [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:50-80](), [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:99-161]()

### RMS Normalization (RMSNorm)

Standard RMS normalization computes mean square over the last dimension with reciprocal-square-root scaling [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-69](). By contrast, the Gemma family initializes norm weights to zero and applies them via `1.0 + weight` [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-80]().

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-69](), [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-80]()

### SwiGLU MLP (Feed-Forward Layer)

Architectures like Mistral, Gemma, and Gemma 3 utilize three projections (`gate_proj`, `up_proj`, and `down_proj`) to implement SwiGLU feed-forward networks [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47]().

| Component | Role in MLP |
|---|---|
| `gate_proj` | Projects hidden states to intermediate dimensions and applies activation [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47](). |
| `up_proj` | Projects hidden states for elementwise combination [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47](). |
| `down_proj` | Maps the gated intermediate representation back to the model hidden dimension [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47](). |
| `ACT2FN` | Resolves the activation function from the configuration [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47](). |

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47]()

### Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) & Masking

Grouped-Query Attention reduces KV cache memory overhead by sharing key-value heads across multiple query heads. Helper functions like `repeat_kv` expand key/value head counts to match query dimensions during attention score computation [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:120-136](). Models also integrate causal masking and sliding-window attention masks [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:12-31]().

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:83-136]()

---

|---|---|---|---|
| Llama | `LlamaRMSNorm` [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-69]() | Gated MLP | `LlamaRotaryEmbedding`, `apply_rotary_pos_emb` [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:72-149]() |
| Mistral | Standard RMSNorm | `MistralMLP` (SwiGLU) [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-47]() | GQA with `repeat_kv` [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:83-136]() |
| Gemma | `GemmaRMSNorm` (`1.0 + weight`) [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-80]() | `GemmaMLP` (SwiGLU) [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:83-96]() | `GemmaRotaryEmbedding` [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:99-161]() |

Sources: [src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py:51-149](), [src/transformers/models/mistral/modeling_mistral.py:34-136](), [src/transformers/models/gemma/modeling_gemma.py:63-161]()

# Page: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Models

# Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Models

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) implementation patterns visible in the Transformers source: router decisions, stacked expert weights, expert execution, auxiliary-loss outputs, and expert-parallel-aware dispatch. The model-specific examples below cover Llama4, GraniteMoE, JetMoE, DeepSeek-V3/V4, GLM-MoE-DSA, and DBRX where source excerpts show relevant implementation details. 

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py`  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py`  
`src/transformers/models/jetmoe/modeling_jetmoe.py`  
`src/transformers/models/deepseek_v3/modeling_deepseek_v3.py`  
`src/transformers/models/deepseek_v4/modular_deepseek_v4.py`  
`src/transformers/models/glm_moe_dsa/modular_glm_moe_dsa.py`  
`src/transformers/models/dbrx/modeling_dbrx.py`

---

## Architecture Overview

MoE replaces a dense feed-forward computation with a router and multiple expert feed-forward networks. A router scores experts for each token; the selected experts process routed token states, and their outputs are weighted and combined. Concrete implementations differ: Granite separates routing decisions from expert execution, Llama4 uses sigmoid scores and a shared MLP, and the general integration utility represents routing as flattened token–expert pairs for batched matrix multiplication. 

### Core components: natural-language concepts to code entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["Token hidden states"] --> Router["GraniteMoeTopKRouter.forward"]
    Input --> LlamaRouter["Llama4Router.forward"]
    Router --> Decisions["router_logits, top_k_weights, top_k_index"]
    LlamaRouter --> Scores["router_scores, router_logits"]
    Decisions --> Experts["GraniteMoeExperts"]
    Scores --> LlamaMoe["Llama4TextMoe"]
    Experts --> Backend["use_experts_implementation"]
    LlamaMoe --> LlamaExperts["Llama4TextExperts"]
    Backend --> Output["Weighted expert output"]
    LlamaExperts --> Output
```

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py:113-145`  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:140-171`

### Data path through a routed layer

In GraniteMoE, `GraniteMoeTopKRouter.forward` computes logits, selects the top-k experts, and applies softmax to the selected logits. It returns logits, weights, and indices; its class documentation places grouping and scattering inside the expert forward path rather than in the router. 

In the shared batched-matrix-multiplication implementation, `batched_mm_experts_forward` repeats each token state once per selected expert, flattens routing weights and expert IDs, selects the corresponding projection weights, applies the expert activation or gate, then selects down-projection weights. 

Llama4 takes a different route: `Llama4TextMoe.forward` flattens the hidden states, obtains router scores, repeats token inputs across routed slots, scales those inputs, invokes `Llama4TextExperts`, and also computes a `shared_expert` MLP output. 

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py:113-132`  
`src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:112-159`  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:155-171`

---

## 1. Router and Expert Selection

A router maps each token’s hidden state to scores over experts. Implementations use different score transformations and may return different combinations of raw logits, selected weights, and selected indices. 

### Llama4Router

`Llama4Router` is an `nn.Linear` projection from `hidden_size` to `num_local_experts`, with no bias. Its forward pass selects `top_k` logits, scatters the selected values into a tensor whose other entries are negative infinity, applies sigmoid in float32, and returns scores together with the original router logits. 

### GraniteMoeTopKRouter

`GraniteMoeTopKRouter` computes logits with `F.linear`, selects the top-k logits per token, and applies softmax over those selected logits. It returns `(router_logits, top_k_weights, top_k_index)`. The class documentation states that token grouping and scattering happen in the expert forward path, allowing the default `grouped_mm` and `batched_mm` paths to compile without the former `expert_size.tolist()` operation in the router. 

### DeepseekV3TopkRouter

`DeepseekV3TopkRouter` computes float32 router logits, applies sigmoid scores, adds an expert correction bias for selection, and groups experts before selecting groups and experts. Its constructor records routing settings including `top_k`, group counts, normalization behavior, routed scaling, and the correction-bias buffer. 

### Router flow: natural-language concepts to code entities

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Hidden["hidden_states"] --> Granite["GraniteMoeTopKRouter.forward"]
    Hidden --> Llama["Llama4Router.forward"]
    Hidden --> Deepseek["DeepseekV3TopkRouter.forward"]
    Granite --> GOut["router_logits, top_k_weights, top_k_index"]
    Llama --> LOut["router_scores, router_logits"]
    Deepseek --> DLogits["float32 router_logits"]
    DLogits --> DSigmoid["sigmoid scores plus e_score_correction_bias"]
    DSigmoid --> Groups["group_scores, group_idx, group_mask"]
```

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py:113-132`  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:140-151`  
`src/transformers/models/deepseek_v3/modeling_deepseek_v3.py:120-150`

---

## 2. Expert Weight Stacking and Computation

Stacking expert parameters along an expert dimension allows implementations to select or batch expert weights without representing every expert as an independent module. The specific tensor layouts vary by model and operation. 

### Llama4TextExperts

`Llama4TextExperts` stores `gate_up_proj` and `down_proj` as expert-indexed parameters. Its forward method reshapes the supplied states to an expert-major layout, performs batched matrix multiplication for the combined gate/up projection, splits the result into gate and up components, applies the activation to the gate, multiplies by the up component, and applies the batched down projection. 

`Llama4TextMoe` calls the router and expert collection, and includes a separate `shared_expert` MLP. The excerpt shows the shared MLP result being computed alongside the routed output; it does not show the subsequent combination lines, so this page does not infer the exact combination operation. 

### GraniteMoeExperts

`GraniteMoeExperts` is decorated with `@use_experts_implementation` and stores `gate_up_proj` and `down_proj` as three-dimensional parameters indexed by expert. This decorator makes the class a consumer of the configurable expert implementation mechanism. 

### JetMoeParallelExperts

`JetMoeParallelExperts` stores weights in `[num_experts, output_size, input_size]` layout. Its forward method splits the input according to `expert_size`, applies `F.linear` with each expert’s weight, and concatenates the resulting outputs. 

### Shared batched dispatch utility

`batched_mm_experts_forward` models routing as `S = num_tokens * num_top_k` selected token–expert pairs. It repeats token states with `repeat_interleave`, flattens the weights and IDs, selects the expert projection weights, then applies either `_apply_gate` or `act_fn` depending on whether the expert has a gate. 

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    States["hidden_states"] --> Repeat["repeat_interleave(num_top_k)"]
    Indices["top_k_index"] --> FlattenIds["expert_ids"]
    Weights["top_k_weights"] --> FlattenWeights["sample_weights"]
    Repeat --> Select["Select per-pair expert weights"]
    FlattenIds --> Select
    Select --> Up["Batched up projection via _batched_linear"]
    Up --> Gate["Apply _apply_gate or act_fn"]
    Gate --> Down["Select and apply down_proj"]
```

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:54-83`  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:155-171`  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py:135-145`  
`src/transformers/models/jetmoe/modeling_jetmoe.py:115-157`  
`src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:112-157`

---

## 3. Load-Balancing Auxiliary Loss

Router outputs are part of the model-facing interface used to expose routing information. `Llama4Router` returns raw logits alongside router scores, and `GraniteMoeTopKRouter` returns logits, selected weights, and selected expert indices. 

The supplied excerpts do not show the loss calculation or the model call site that consumes router outputs to compute an auxiliary load-balancing loss. Consequently, this page identifies the router outputs but does not specify a loss formula or claim which of the listed models computes that loss. 

Sources:  
`src/transformers/models/llama4/modeling_llama4.py:146-151`  
`src/transformers/models/granitemoe/modeling_granitemoe.py:128-132`

---

## 4. Expert Parallelism

`batched_mm_experts_forward` contains an explicit expert-parallel branch. When `self._is_expert_parallel` is true, it marks expert IDs greater than or equal to `self.num_experts` as sentinels and clamps IDs into the local expert range before indexing projection weights. The code comments explain that routing weights for sentinel slots are already zeroed by `RouterParallel` at dispatch, so those contributions are removed by weighted multiplication, though the batched matrix multiplication still performs wasted work for the clamped slots. 

The cited excerpt documents local sentinel handling; it does not show the full distributed token-dispatch or communication implementation. 

Sources:  
`src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:128-136`

---

## 5. Model-Specific Implementation Patterns

| Model or family | Code entities evidenced in the supplied excerpts | Implementation detail supported by the excerpt |
|---|---|---|
| Llama4 | `Llama4Router`, `Llama4TextExperts`, `Llama4TextMoe` | Sigmoid-scored top-k routing; stacked expert projections; routed and shared MLP paths. |
| GraniteMoE | `GraniteMoeTopKRouter`, `GraniteMoeExperts` | Top-k softmax routing returns logits, weights, and indices; expert class uses `use_experts_implementation`. |
| JetMoE | `JetMoeParallelExperts` | Expert-indexed `[num_experts, output_size, input_size]` weights and split-per-expert linear computation. |
| DeepSeek-V3 | `DeepseekV3TopkRouter` | Sigmoid scores, expert correction bias, and grouped expert selection. |
| DeepSeek-V4 | `DeepseekV4Experts` is imported by the modular model | The supplied modular excerpt shows the expert class import and reuse of Mixtral classes, but not the V4 expert forward implementation. |
| GLM-MoE-DSA | `GlmMoeDsaConfig` | Configuration exposes routed and shared expert counts, experts per token, routing scale, group settings, and dense/sparse MLP-layer options. |
| DBRX | `modeling_dbrx.py` | The provided excerpt establishes that this generated modeling file is derived from `modular_dbrx.py`; it does not include the DBRX router or expert implementation. |

The DeepSeek-V4 modular source imports `MixtralExperts`, `MixtralForCausalLM`, `MixtralPreTrainedModel`, and `MixtralTopKRouter`, showing reuse of those named implementation entities in that module. The excerpt alone does not establish which imported entities are used by a specific V4 forward path. 

The GLM-MoE-DSA configuration declares `n_shared_experts`, `n_routed_experts`, `num_experts_per_tok`, `routed_scaling_factor`, `n_group`, and `topk_group`; it also documents an MLP-layer pattern that distinguishes dense and sparse layers.

## 6. Expert Backends and Kernel Integration

The shared MoE integration module imports expert forward implementations named `deepgemm_bf16_experts_forward` and `sonicmoe_experts_forward`. It also defines `batched_mm_experts_forward`, which provides a batched matrix-multiplication path over selected token–expert pairs. 

`GraniteMoeExperts` uses `@use_experts_implementation`, providing a model-level integration point for selecting an expert implementation. DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-MoE-DSA import the same integration decorator in their modeling modules, although the supplied excerpts do not show its application to their expert classes.

# State Space & Hybrid Models

## Purpose and scope

This page describes the state-space recurrence and hybrid-layer patterns visible in the supplied Transformers model implementations. It focuses on Mamba and Mamba2 recurrence, kernel-backed and PyTorch paths, and hybrid-model components such as Jamba attention and `GraniteMoeHybridAttention`. The model families in scope also include Bamba, FalconMamba/H1, Zamba, NemotronH, Qwen3-Next, LFM2, xLSTM, and RWKV; however, the supplied excerpts do not expose enough of each implementation to document their layer layouts or call paths in detail. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:48-57](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:73-90](), [src/transformers/models/jamba/modeling_jamba.py:128-155](), [src/transformers/models/granitemoehybrid/modeling_granitemoehybrid.py:121-146]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:48-57](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:73-90](), [src/transformers/models/jamba/modeling_jamba.py:128-155](), [src/transformers/models/granitemoehybrid/modeling_granitemoehybrid.py:121-146]()

---

## SSM Recurrence and Selective State Spaces

A selective state-space layer maintains a recurrent state and derives an output from that state. In the Mamba implementation, `mamba_selective_state_update` adjusts the timestep with an optional bias and softplus, computes discretized transition and input terms, updates the stored state, and projects it with `C`. It can then add the optional `D` skip connection and apply an optional SiLU gate `z`. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170]()

For sequence-wide processing, `mamba_selective_scan` accepts the sequence inputs and SSM parameters. Its visible implementation prepares optional scan implementations, applies the timestep bias and softplus, and transposes `B` and `C` for the expected kernel layout. The provided excerpt ends before the remainder of the scan computation, so it does not establish the full dispatch or return behavior. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:173-212]()

### Recurrent update data flow

**Diagram: From recurrent input to updated SSM state**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["hidden_states"] --> Step["dt plus optional dt_bias"]
    Step --> Softplus["optional F.softplus"]
    Step --> Transition["dA = exp(dt * A)"]
    Softplus --> Transition
    Softplus --> InputTerm["dB = dt * B"]
    InputTerm --> StateInput["dBx = dB * hidden_states"]
    Transition --> State["ssm_state = state * dA + dBx"]
    StateInput --> State
    State --> Save["state.copy_"]
    State --> Readout["C readout"]
    Input --> Skip["optional D skip"]
    Readout --> Output["out"]
    Skip --> Output
    Output --> Gate["optional SiLU(z) gate"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170]()

### Sequence processing, padding, and chunk helpers

The Mamba and FalconMamba implementations expose `causal_conv1d_fn` for causal grouped 1D convolution and `causal_conv1d_update` for convolution that carries a rolling `conv_state`. Both functions optionally apply an activation after convolution. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:75-115]()

`apply_mask_to_padding_states` zeros hidden states at masked positions using the two-dimensional attention mask. Mamba2 and NemotronH also provide chunk helpers: `pad_tensor_by_size` pads the sequence dimension, `reshape_into_chunks` groups padded sequences into chunks, and `segment_sum` constructs a stable lower-triangular cumulative sum representation. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:48-57](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:42-90](), [src/transformers/models/nemotron_h/modeling_nemotron_h.py:79-127]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:48-57](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:75-115](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:42-90](), [src/transformers/models/nemotron_h/modeling_nemotron_h.py:79-127]()

---

## Mamba & Mamba2 Architectures

### Mamba

Mamba’s modeling module defines causal-convolution helpers, the recurrent update `mamba_selective_state_update`, and the sequence function `mamba_selective_scan`. The convolution helpers provide a causal grouped-convolution operation and a stateful update path; the recurrent update discretizes the transition and input terms, mutates the supplied state, and forms the output from `C`, with optional `D` and `z` contributions. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170]()

The module decorates the convolution and SSM helper functions with Hub-kernel fallback decorators. The visible excerpt establishes the decorated function names and the fallback identifiers, but does not show the complete model-level dispatch path. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-61](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:80-81](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:103-104](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-128](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:173-174]()

### Mamba2

Mamba2 includes sequence chunking helpers and `MambaRMSNormGated`. Its `segment_sum` expands the input along a new dimension, masks the upper triangle, computes cumulative sums, then masks the result to retain the lower-triangular region. [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:73-90](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:105-120]()

The file declares `mamba2_split_conv1d_scan_combined`, decorated to use the `mamba_split_conv1d_scan_combined` Hub function with `mamba_ssm` fallback. The supplied excerpt shows the function signature and initial arguments, but not its implementation or the model call site; therefore, no further claims about its exact fusion behavior are made here. [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:166-175]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:103-128](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-188](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:42-90](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:105-120](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:166-175]()

### Mamba processing path

The following diagram summarizes the visible helper-level flow: causal convolution produces features for SSM processing; the recurrent update uses `dt`, `A`, `B`, `C`, and optional `D` and `z`. It does not assert a model-level call order that is not visible in the supplied excerpts. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-188]()

**Diagram: Mamba helper-level convolution and recurrence**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["hidden_states"] --> Conv["causal_conv1d_fn"]
    Conv --> ScanInput["SSM sequence input"]
    ScanInput --> Scan["mamba_selective_scan"]
    Input --> Update["mamba_selective_state_update"]
    Parameters["dt, A, B, C"] --> Update
    Update --> State["updated recurrent state"]
    Update --> Readout["C readout"]
    Readout --> Optional["optional D skip and SiLU(z)"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-100](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-188]()

## Hybrid Attention-SSM Models

Hybrid architectures combine state-space components with attention or other layer types. The supplied excerpts show attention implementation details for Jamba and GraniteMoEHybrid, as well as Zamba’s attention dimensions and its dependence on concatenated hidden states. They do not include the model-level layer-selection loops or configuration-driven interleaving logic for these architectures. [src/transformers/models/jamba/modeling_jamba.py:128-155](), [src/transformers/models/granitemoehybrid/modeling_granitemoehybrid.py:96-146](), [src/transformers/models/zamba/modeling_zamba.py:114-145]()

### Jamba, Bamba & FalconMamba/H1

The visible Jamba excerpt defines `JambaAttention` and an eager attention helper. The helper repeats key/value heads when needed, computes scaled query-key weights, adds an optional attention mask, applies softmax and dropout, and multiplies by values. The provided lines do not show Jamba’s SSM mixer or the model’s layer-interleaving code. [src/transformers/models/jamba/modeling_jamba.py:128-155]()

The Bamba modeling excerpt defines `BambaRotaryEmbedding`, including RoPE parameter initialization and cosine/sine generation. It also provides attention helpers; the supplied lines do not expose Bamba’s SSM mixer or layer schedule. [src/transformers/models/bamba/modeling_bamba.py:50-96](), [src/transformers/models/bamba/modeling_bamba.py:106-140]()

FalconMamba defines `FalconMambaWeightlessRMSNorm`, whose normalized output is computed in float and converted back to the input dtype. Its excerpt also shows the causal convolution helpers and recurrent-update function. Falcon H1 is listed among the broader family scope, but its implementation details are not present in the supplied excerpts. [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:46-60](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:75-115](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:142-185]()

### Zamba, Zamba2 & NemotronH

Zamba’s `ZambaAttention` consumes `attention_hidden_size`, and the class documentation describes its input as the concatenation of original hidden states and output from a preceding Mamba layer. Its projections create query, key, and value tensors, and its scaling is based on half the attention head dimension. [src/transformers/models/zamba/modeling_zamba.py:114-145]()

Zamba2 defines `Zamba2RMSNormGated`, which optionally multiplies the input by `SiLU(gate)`, reshapes its last dimension into groups, and normalizes each group. NemotronH defines a corresponding `NemotronHRMSNormGated` with the same visible pattern of optional gating and grouped RMS normalization. [src/transformers/models/zamba2/modeling_zamba2.py:50-68](), [src/transformers/models/nemotron_h/modeling_nemotron_h.py:55-73]()

### GraniteMoEHybrid and other listed families

`GraniteMoeHybridAttention` is an attention module with query, key, value, and output projections. Its class documentation explicitly covers the case where `position_embeddings is None`, allowing configurations to opt out of RoPE. The available excerpt does not show the model’s SSM module or its layer-interleaving schedule. [src/transformers/models/granitemoehybrid/modeling_granitemoehybrid.py:121-146]()

Qwen3-Next, LFM2, xLSTM, and RWKV are included in this page’s scope, but their modeling excerpts are not supplied. The same applies to detailed model-level interleaving claims for Bamba, Jamba, Zamba2, and NemotronH. Their layer schedules should be documented from their respective model and configuration implementations rather than inferred from the helper excerpts available here.

Sources: [src/transformers/models/jamba/modeling_jamba.py:128-155](), [src/transformers/models/bamba/modeling_bamba.py:50-96](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:46-60](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:75-115](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:142-185](), [src/transformers/models/zamba/modeling_zamba.py:114-145](), [src/transformers/models/zamba2/modeling_zamba2.py:50-68](), [src/transformers/models/nemotron_h/modeling_nemotron_h.py:55-73](), [src/transformers/models/granitemoehybrid/modeling_granitemoehybrid.py:121-146]()

## Implementation Details

### Optional kernel integration

The Mamba and FalconMamba modules decorate convolution and SSM helper functions with `use_kernel_func_from_hub_with_fallback`. The visible decorators name Hub functions and fallback packages, including `causal_conv1d_update`, `causal_conv1d_fn`, `mamba_inner_fn`, `selective_state_update`, and `selective_scan_fn`. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-61](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:80-81](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:103-104](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-128](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:173-174](), [src/transformers/models/falcon_mamba/modeling_falcon_mamba.py:75-76]()

Mamba2 similarly decorates `mamba2_split_conv1d_scan_combined` with a Hub-kernel fallback. Since the excerpt does not include the full function body or call site, the precise runtime choice and fused operations are not described here. [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:166-175]()

### Cache and state management

The Mamba and Mamba2 modules import `Cache` and `DynamicCache`, and their modeling modules expose recurrent and convolutional state helper functions. In the visible recurrent update, the state is updated in place with `state.copy_`; in the convolution update, `conv_state` is refreshed from the latest rolling window. These excerpts establish state mutation at the helper level, but do not show the complete model cache structure or how hybrid attention KV caches are coordinated with SSM states. [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:25-30](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-170](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-77](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:25-31](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:123-140]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:25-30](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:60-77](), [src/transformers/models/mamba/modeling_mamba.py:127-188](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:25-31](), [src/transformers/models/mamba2/modeling_mamba2.py:123-175]()

# Page: Encoder-Decoder & Sequence-to-Sequence Models

# Encoder-Decoder & Sequence-to-Sequence Models

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the encoder-decoder pattern used for sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) tasks: an encoder represents the input, and an autoregressive decoder produces output tokens conditioned on those representations. It focuses on cross-attention, decoder input preparation, caching, and the model families in scope: T5, BART, mBART, Marian, Pegasus, M2M-100, NLLB, SwitchTransformers, LongT5, UDOP, and T5Gemma. The supplied implementation excerpts provide details for BART, SwitchTransformers, UDOP, and T5Gemma; T5 is represented here by its model tests.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:94-141](), [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:52-110](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130]()

## Core architecture overview

### Encoder-decoder data flow

In a seq2seq model, the encoder processes source tokens into hidden states. The decoder processes target-prefix tokens with causal self-attention and uses cross-attention to condition its hidden states on the encoder output. Model outputs commonly include a sequence-to-sequence output structure; UDOP’s imports, for example, include `Seq2SeqLMOutput` and `Seq2SeqModelOutput`.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:30-50](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

**Diagram: Source and target sequence flow**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SourceText["Source text"] --> InputIds["input_ids"]
    InputIds --> Encoder["Encoder"]
    Encoder --> EncoderStates["encoder_hidden_states"]
    TargetPrefix["decoder_input_ids"] --> DecoderSelfAttention["Decoder self-attention"]
    EncoderStates --> CrossAttention["Decoder cross-attention"]
    DecoderSelfAttention --> CrossAttention
    CrossAttention --> DecoderStates["Decoder hidden states"]
    DecoderStates --> Logits["Vocabulary logits"]
    Logits --> GeneratedText["Generated output tokens"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

### Decoder input preparation

For BART, `shift_tokens_right` constructs decoder inputs by copying the labels one position to the right, placing `decoder_start_token_id` at position zero, and replacing shifted `-100` values with `pad_token_id`. It raises an error if `pad_token_id` is undefined. This aligns the decoder input at each position with the next-token prediction objective.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71]()

The T5 test fixture separately prepares encoder `input_ids`, `decoder_input_ids`, masks for each sequence, and optional language-model labels. Its config includes encoder/decoder layer counts and `decoder_start_token_id`, making the separate source and target sequence lengths explicit in the test setup.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-82](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:150-166]()

### Embeddings and configuration

BART defines `BartLearnedPositionalEmbedding`, which adds an offset of two to position indices, and `BartScaledWordEmbedding`, which multiplies token embeddings by a configured scale. These are model-specific embedding behaviors rather than requirements of the general encoder-decoder pattern.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:74-98](), [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:101-112]()

T5’s test config includes `d_model`, `d_ff`, attention head count, relative-attention bucket count, encoder and decoder layer counts, and special-token IDs. The fixture also captures a T5 v1.1 configuration variant with `feed_forward_proj="gated-gelu"` and `tie_word_embeddings=False`.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:150-188]()

T5Gemma represents the encoder and decoder with separate `T5GemmaModuleConfig` configurations inside `T5GemmaConfig`. During post-initialization, it marks the encoder as non-decoder and the decoder as decoder, enables decoder caching, and sets the decoder’s `cross_attention_hidden_size` from the encoder hidden size. The top-level configuration declares `is_encoder_decoder=True` and exposes `tie_word_embeddings`.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:67-88](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:92-141]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-112](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:67-141](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-188]()

## Cross-attention and caching

Cross-attention uses decoder states to form queries and encoder states as the source of keys and values. The supplied T5Gemma modular implementation defines `T5GemmaCrossAttention` as a `Gemma2Attention` subclass, disables causal attention for that module, requires `cross_attention_hidden_size`, and creates key/value projections with that input size. This makes the encoder-to-decoder hidden-size relationship explicit.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:171-186]()

UDOP’s `BaseModelOutputWithAttentionMask` documents `past_key_values` as a cache that can contain self-attention key/value states and, for encoder-decoder models, cross-attention key/value states. It also defines optional `attentions` and `cross_attentions` output fields.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

**Diagram: Cross-attention inputs and cached states**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DecoderStates["Decoder hidden states"] --> Queries["Cross-attention queries"]
    EncoderStates["Encoder hidden states"] --> KeyProjection["Cross-attention key projection"]
    EncoderStates --> ValueProjection["Cross-attention value projection"]
    Queries --> CrossAttention["T5GemmaCrossAttention"]
    KeyProjection --> CrossAttention
    ValueProjection --> CrossAttention
    CrossAttention --> Context["Contextualized decoder states"]
    CrossAttention -.-> PastKeyValues["past_key_values"]
    PastKeyValues -.-> CrossAttention
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:171-186](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

### BART attention building blocks

`BartAttention` has separate `q_proj`, `k_proj`, and `v_proj` linear projections, checks that the embedding dimension is divisible by the number of attention heads, and stores the per-head scaling factor. Its constructor also carries decoder, causal, and layer-index parameters; a decoder attention instance without `layer_idx` emits a warning when caching is relevant.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:143-182]()

BART’s `eager_attention_forward` computes scaled query-key scores, adds an optional attention mask, applies softmax and dropout, and multiplies the resulting weights by values.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:114-140]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:114-182](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:171-186](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

## Seq2seq generation and cache behavior

The model implementations shown import `GenerationMixin`, providing the generation integration point used by these architectures. The BART modeling file imports `Cache`, `DynamicCache`, and `EncoderDecoderCache`; UDOP’s output documentation describes `past_key_values` as a way to reuse computed states during sequential decoding.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:24-28](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:36-40](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-112]()

The T5 test suite imports `GenerationTesterMixin` and the `T5ForConditionalGeneration` class, and its fixture supplies separate encoder and decoder inputs. The BART tests likewise import `GenerationTesterMixin`, `BartForConditionalGeneration`, and `BartModel`. These imports show that the test suites exercise generation-capable model classes; the supplied excerpts do not expose the full generation call path.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:35-55](), [tests/models/bart/test_modeling_bart.py:34-53](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130]()

**Diagram: Generation inputs, model outputs, and cache**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SourceIds["input_ids"] --> Encoder["Encoder"]
    Encoder --> EncoderStates["encoder_hidden_states"]
    DecoderPrefix["decoder_input_ids"] --> Decoder["Decoder"]
    EncoderStates --> Decoder
    Cache["past_key_values"] --> Decoder
    Decoder --> Seq2SeqOutput["Seq2SeqLMOutput"]
    Seq2SeqOutput --> NextToken["Next-token scores"]
    NextToken --> UpdatedPrefix["Updated decoder prefix"]
    UpdatedPrefix --> Decoder
    Decoder -.-> Cache
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132](), [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:24-28](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:24-28](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:36-112](), [tests/models/bart/test_modeling_bart.py:34-53](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:35-55]()

## Model-specific implementation notes

### T5

The T5 test fixture constructs a `T5Config` with separate encoder and decoder layer counts, model and feed-forward dimensions, attention heads, relative-attention bucket count, dropout, and special-token IDs. It prepares `input_ids`, `decoder_input_ids`, encoder and decoder masks, and optional labels. The test module imports `T5Model`, `T5EncoderModel`, and `T5ForConditionalGeneration`.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:45-55](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-82](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:150-166]()

### BART and mBART

The supplied BART implementation defines right-shifting for decoder inputs, learned positional embeddings with an offset, scaled word embeddings, and the `BartAttention` projection layers. The mBART modeling file is listed among the supplied additional files, but its contents are not shown here; implementation details specific to mBART are therefore not inferred.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71](), [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:74-112](), [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:143-182]()

### SwitchTransformers

`SwitchTransformersTop1Router` computes router logits from token hidden states, applies softmax, selects the top-probability expert for each token, and constructs a one-hot dispatch mask. It uses cumulative token priorities to mask assignments that exceed `expert_capacity`; the selected expert probability is returned with the mask and raw router logits.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:52-110]()

`SwitchTransformersLayerNorm` computes the mean square of hidden states in float32, scales by the reciprocal square root of variance plus epsilon, and applies a learned weight. This is a scale-only normalization with no mean subtraction or bias.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:113-135]()

### T5Gemma

`T5GemmaConfig` composes encoder and decoder module configs and sets the decoder’s cross-attention input size from the encoder hidden size. Its modular file also defines T5Gemma-specific RMS normalization and a gated MLP with dropout. The generated `modeling_t5gemma.py` file identifies `modular_t5gemma.py` as its source; the modular file is the appropriate source for edits.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:67-141](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:144-157](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modeling_t5gemma.py:1-5]()

### UDOP

UDOP defines `BaseModelOutputWithAttentionMask`, whose fields include `last_hidden_state`, an attention mask, cache, hidden states, self-attentions, and cross-attentions. The same modeling file imports seq2seq model and language-model output types.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:30-50](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()

### Other listed families

The supplied file list includes modeling paths for Marian, Pegasus, and LongT5, as well as tests for several multilingual and long-sequence variants. Their implementation contents are not shown in the excerpts, so this page does not attribute specific attention algorithms, token-shifting rules, or generation behavior to those files.  
Sources: [src/transformers/models/marian/modeling_marian.py:1-50](), [src/transformers/models/pegasus/modeling_pegasus.py:1-50](), [src/transformers/models/longt5/modeling_longt5.py:1-50]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-182](), [src/transformers/models/longt5/modeling_longt5.py:1-50](), [src/transformers/models/marian/modeling_marian.py:1-50](), [src/transformers/models/pegasus/modeling_pegasus.py:1-50](), [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:52-135](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modeling_t5gemma.py:1-5](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:67-157](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:30-132](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:45-166]()

## Tests as architecture checks

The T5 tests use a `T5ModelTester` fixture to create encoder and decoder inputs, masks, labels, and a config. The test module imports common model, generation, configuration, and pipeline test mixins.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:35-55](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-82](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130]()

The BART tests import `BartModel`, `BartForConditionalGeneration`, `BartEncoder`, `BartDecoder`, and `shift_tokens_right`. Their input helper creates encoder and decoder masks from padding-token comparisons, providing test coverage points for the model’s separate input streams.  
Sources: [tests/models/bart/test_modeling_bart.py:43-53](), [tests/models/bart/test_modeling_bart.py:56-73]()

The T5Gemma and SwitchTransformers test modules import their conditional-generation model classes and `GenerationTesterMixin`, alongside common model and pipeline test mixins.  
Sources: [tests/models/t5gemma/test_modeling_t5gemma.py:32-48](), [tests/models/switch_transformers/test_modeling_switch_transformers.py:29-50]()

Sources: [tests/models/bart/test_modeling_bart.py:43-73](), [tests/models/switch_transformers/test_modeling_switch_transformers.py:29-50](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:35-130](), [tests/models/t5gemma/test_modeling_t5gemma.py:32-48]()

## Summary

- Seq2seq models encode source inputs and condition decoder predictions on encoder representations; UDOP’s output type explicitly exposes cross-attention outputs and cached states.  
  Sources: [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132]()
- BART’s `shift_tokens_right` prepares shifted decoder inputs and handles ignored-label values.  
  Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71]()
- T5 test fixtures make encoder inputs, decoder inputs, masks, labels, and configuration dimensions explicit.  
  Sources: [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-82](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:106-130]()
- T5Gemma’s configuration links decoder cross-attention dimensions to encoder hidden size, and its cross-attention module uses that size for key/value projections.  
  Sources: [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:125-141](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:171-186]()
- SwitchTransformers adds top-1 token routing and expert-capacity masking within its seq2seq model family.  
  Sources: [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:52-110]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/bart/modeling_bart.py:58-71](), [src/transformers/models/switch_transformers/modeling_switch_transformers.py:52-110](), [src/transformers/models/t5gemma/modular_t5gemma.py:125-186](), [src/transformers/models/udop/modeling_udop.py:97-132](), [tests/models/t5/test_modeling_t5.py:58-130]()
