# Page: DeepSpeed & FSDP Integration

# DeepSpeed & FSDP Integration

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.circleci/create_circleci_config.py](.circleci/create_circleci_config.py)

</details>



The purpose and scope of this page is to describe the available implementation details for DeepSpeed configuration integration and PyTorch FSDP in Transformers. It covers DeepSpeed ZeRO configuration, FSDP utilities and distributed configuration, process-group setup, and the FSDP test harness. The provided source excerpts do not show the DeepSpeed-Inference implementation, so this page does not describe its runtime behavior. [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:17-19]()

---

## 1. DeepSpeed Integration

DeepSpeed ZeRO reduces replicated training state by sharding optimizer states, gradients, and parameters across GPUs. ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states; ZeRO-2 additionally shards gradients; ZeRO-3 also shards parameters. The documentation recommends ZeRO-2 when it fits and reserving ZeRO-3 for cases where ZeRO-2 does not fit. [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:17-41]()

### Key Components and Configuration

`is_deepspeed_available()` checks whether the `deepspeed` package can be found and whether its package metadata is available. `HfDeepSpeedConfig` subclasses Accelerate’s `HfDeepSpeedConfig` when both Accelerate and DeepSpeed are available; otherwise it uses `object` as the base class so the module can still be imported. Its initializer registers the config through `set_hf_deepspeed_config()` and checks the Accelerate and DeepSpeed dependency versions. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:36-55](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:57-80]()

A weak reference to the active config is retained so code outside the `Trainer` can query DeepSpeed settings, including during model-loading operations. The Trainer-specific subclass, `HfTrainerDeepSpeedConfig`, is intended to live as long as `TrainingArguments`; it tracks the dtype and configuration mismatches. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:57-67](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:82-103]()

`HfTrainerDeepSpeedConfig.fill_match()` replaces a DeepSpeed `"auto"` value with the corresponding Hugging Face value. For explicit values, it records mismatches when `must_match=True`; `fill_only` is the partial method variant that fills `"auto"` values without requiring a match. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:98-131]()

`trainer_config_process()` computes the aggregate training batch size as `world_size × per_device_train_batch_size × gradient_accumulation_steps`, then synchronizes or checks DeepSpeed entries for micro-batch size, accumulation steps, total batch size, gradient clipping, optimizer parameters, and scheduler learning-rate values. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:133-171]()

The user-facing documentation describes passing a DeepSpeed JSON config through `TrainingArguments.deepspeed`; it recommends `"auto"` for values that should be filled from `TrainingArguments`. It also documents DeepSpeed, `torchrun`, and Accelerate launch options. [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:54-105]()

| DeepSpeed config entry | Hugging Face value used by `trainer_config_process()` |
|---|---|
| `train_micro_batch_size_per_gpu` | `per_device_train_batch_size` |
| `gradient_accumulation_steps` | `gradient_accumulation_steps` |
| `train_batch_size` | Computed from world size, per-device batch size, and accumulation steps |
| `gradient_clipping` | `max_grad_norm` |
| `optimizer.params.lr` | `learning_rate` |
| `optimizer.params.betas` | `adam_beta1`, `adam_beta2` |
| `optimizer.params.eps` | `adam_epsilon` |
| `optimizer.params.weight_decay` | `weight_decay` |
| `scheduler.params.warmup_max_lr` | `learning_rate` |

The mappings and total-batch-size calculation are implemented in `trainer_config_process()`. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:138-171]()

### DeepSpeed Configuration Data Flow

**Diagram: `TrainingArguments` values into `HfTrainerDeepSpeedConfig`**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Natural Language Inputs"
        TA["TrainingArguments"]
        JSON["DeepSpeed JSON config"]
    end
    subgraph "Code entities"
        HDC["HfTrainerDeepSpeedConfig"]
        PROCESS["trainer_config_process()"]
        MATCH["fill_match()"]
        RUNTIME["DeepSpeed runtime"]
    end
    TA --> PROCESS
    JSON --> HDC
    HDC --> PROCESS
    PROCESS --> MATCH
    MATCH -->|"replace auto values or record mismatches"| HDC
    HDC --> RUNTIME
```

`HfTrainerDeepSpeedConfig` initializes from the supplied config, and `trainer_config_process()` uses `fill_match()` to synchronize selected config values with `TrainingArguments`. The documentation describes the resulting config as the one passed to the DeepSpeed training integration. [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:82-103](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:105-171](), [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:54-61]()

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:36-80](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepspeed.py:82-171](), [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:17-41](), [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:54-105]()

---

## 2. PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) Integration

The native distributed configuration exposes an FSDP size, plan, CPU offload flag, and mixed-precision flag. In `DistributedConfig`, `fsdp_size` defaults to 1, and an `fsdp_plan` is applied only when `fsdp_size > 1`. The documented native configuration refers to FSDP2; `distributed/fsdp.py` imports PyTorch’s composable `fully_shard` and defines FSDP policy helpers. [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-77](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:32-42]()

### Core Implementation (`src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py`)

`ALL_FSDP_STYLES` defines two plan styles: `free_full_weight` and `keep_full_weight`. The module’s `is_fsdp_enabled()` checks whether distributed execution is initialized and whether the Accelerate FSDP environment flags are enabled; the docstring specifies this check covers FSDP1. `is_fsdp_managed_module()` recognizes either a module marked `_is_fsdp_managed_module` or a PyTorch `FullyShardedDataParallel` wrapper. [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:41-65]()

`_get_fsdp_policy_kwargs()` translates `DistributedConfig` runtime flags into arguments for FSDP’s `fully_shard`: CPU offload selects `CPUOffloadPolicy`, while mixed precision selects `MixedPrecisionPolicy` with BF16 parameters and FP32 reductions. [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:68-82]()

For models with tied input embeddings and output heads, `_resolve_tied_embed_lm_head_plan()` examines `all_tied_weights_keys`, locates the embedding and head modules, and adapts the plan so the tied modules are not wrapped as separate FSDP targets. [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:85-146]()

`DistributedMixin` owns the model-level `_fsdp_plan` and exposes it through `fsdp_plan`. Its plan setter accepts `None` as an empty plan, requires a dictionary otherwise, and validates plan styles against `ALL_FSDP_STYLES`. `init_parallel_plans()` copies class-level plans onto the model instance and merges configuration and child-module contributions. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:58-69](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:79-105](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:116-119](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:146-155]()

### FSDP Configuration and Plan Flow

**Diagram: `DistributedConfig` and FSDP plan entities**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Natural Language Inputs"
        CONFIG["Native distributed configuration"]
        TIED["Tied embedding and output-head weights"]
    end
    subgraph "Code entities"
        DC["DistributedConfig"]
        MIXIN["DistributedMixin"]
        PLAN["fsdp_plan"]
        RESOLVE["_resolve_tied_embed_lm_head_plan()"]
        POLICY["_get_fsdp_policy_kwargs()"]
        SHARD["apply_fully_sharded_data_parallelism()"]
    end
    CONFIG --> DC
    DC -->|"fsdp_size, fsdp_plan, offload, mixed precision"| MIXIN
    MIXIN --> PLAN
    TIED --> RESOLVE
    PLAN --> RESOLVE
    DC --> POLICY
    RESOLVE --> SHARD
    POLICY --> SHARD
```

`DistributedConfig` defines the FSDP size, plan, offload, and mixed-precision controls; `DistributedMixin` stores and validates the model plan. The FSDP module contains helpers for policy kwargs and tied-weight plan resolution, and defines `apply_fully_sharded_data_parallelism()`. [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-77](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:58-69](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:146-155](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:68-82](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:111-146](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:176-181]()

Sources: [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:32-82](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:85-181](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:58-105](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:116-155](), [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-77]()

---

## 3. Multi-GPU Training Initialization and Backend Setup

`distributed/utils.py` provides backend selection and process-group helpers used by Transformers’ native distributed infrastructure. The backend map associates CUDA with NCCL, CPU with Gloo, XPU with XCCL, HPU with HCCL, Neuron with `neuron`, and TPU with `tpu_dist`. `get_distributed_backend()` returns the corresponding backend or raises `ValueError` when the device type has no mapping. [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:84-100]()

`_ensure_torch_distributed()` initializes a process group only when one is not already initialized. It reads `RANK`, `LOCAL_RANK`, and `WORLD_SIZE`, selects the backend, binds accelerator devices before initialization where applicable, and calls `torch.distributed.init_process_group()` with a two-hour timeout. On initialization errors, it raises an `OSError` explaining that distributed initialization failed. [_ensure_torch_distributed()` is defined at `src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:112-149](). [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:112-149]()

`_distributed_barrier()` returns immediately if distributed execution is not initialized. Otherwise, it calls `torch.distributed.barrier()` and supplies the current accelerator device ID for non-CPU execution. [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:151-165]()

### Initialization and Distributed Checkpoint Context

`TransformersDeviceMesh` documents distinct dense and expert mesh views over the same ranks: dense parameters use `(pp, fsdp, tp)`, while experts use `(pp, efsdp, ep)`. The corresponding sizes satisfy `pp × fsdp × tp == pp × efsdp × ep`; the documented relationship is `efsdp = fsdp × tp / ep`. [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:167-182]()

`DistributedMixin` imports distributed checkpoint loading, saving, and consolidation helpers, alongside the FSDP and tensor-parallel application functions. Its `prepare_distribute_model()` entry point accepts a `DistributedConfig` and device map, while the shown excerpt establishes its no-config return path. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:29-48](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:167-174]()

The available material does not include the implementation of distributed checkpoint operations or the complete body of `prepare_distribute_model()`. Accordingly, the diagram below limits the flow to the visible configuration and initialization entities. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:29-48](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:167-174]()

**Diagram: distributed configuration to process-group setup**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Natural Language Inputs"
        ENV["RANK, LOCAL_RANK, WORLD_SIZE"]
        DEVICE["Current accelerator or device type"]
        DISTCFG["Distributed parallel configuration"]
    end
    subgraph "Code entities"
        INIT["_ensure_torch_distributed()"]
        BACKEND["get_distributed_backend()"]
        GROUP["torch.distributed.init_process_group()"]
        MESH["TransformersDeviceMesh"]
        BARRIER["_distributed_barrier()"]
        MIXIN["DistributedMixin.prepare_distribute_model()"]
    end
    ENV --> INIT
    DEVICE --> INIT
    INIT --> BACKEND
    BACKEND --> GROUP
    DISTCFG --> MIXIN
    GROUP --> MESH
    MESH --> MIXIN
    GROUP --> BARRIER
```

The process-group helper reads rank environment variables, selects a backend through `get_distributed_backend()`, and initializes the group. `TransformersDeviceMesh` represents the documented parallel mesh axes; `DistributedMixin.prepare_distribute_model()` is a distributed-model orchestration entry point. [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:84-100](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:112-165](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:167-182](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:167-174]()

Sources: [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:84-100](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:102-165](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:167-182](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:29-48](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:167-174]()

## 4. Specialized Weight Loading for DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 and FSDP

The DeepSpeed documentation warns that ZeRO-3 shards parameters during initialization. It instructs users to instantiate `TrainingArguments` before loading the model; loading a full model onto every GPU before DeepSpeed is configured does not save memory. The documented ZeRO-3 configuration includes options such as communication overlap, contiguous gradients, and gathering 16-bit weights on model save. [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:172-187]()

For Transformers’ native distributed path, `DistributedMixin` imports distributed checkpoint load/save and consolidation helpers. The `DistributedConfig` and device-mesh utilities describe the native parallel configuration and mesh, but the supplied excerpts do not show enough of checkpoint loading or the FSDP application function to detail their weight-by-weight data flow. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:29-48](), [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-64](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:167-182](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:176-181]()

Sources: [docs/source/en/deepspeed.md:172-187](), [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:29-48](), [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-64](), [src/transformers/distributed/utils.py:167-182](), [src/transformers/distributed/fsdp.py:176-181]()

---

## 5. Distributed Training and Inference Testing Suite

`tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py` supplies an FSDP testing harness. It defines representative model types for distributed FSDP tests, chooses available workers based on the distributed device type, and sets deterministic execution settings. Its global wrapper sets rank-related environment variables, initializes a process group, invokes the test function, aggregates failures across ranks, writes a result file on rank 0, and destroys the process group after synchronization. [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:79-111](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:142-184]()

The harness also provides a deterministic model-directory setup: rank 0 seeds and constructs a causal language model from config, saves it to a temporary directory, and synchronizes ranks before yielding the directory. [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:114-139]()

The provided test excerpt shows the FSDP harness setup and constants, but not the later test cases. It therefore supports describing the harness mechanics, not specific assertions about training or checkpoint correctness. [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:15-48](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:66-139](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:142-184]()

**Diagram: FSDP test process lifecycle**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    TEST["FSDP test case"]
    WRAP["_fsdp_global_wrapper()"]
    ENV["WORLD_SIZE, RANK, LOCAL_RANK"]
    DEVICE["_set_rank_device()"]
    GROUP["dist.init_process_group()"]
    CALL["func(rank, ...)"]
    REDUCE["dist.all_reduce(error_flag)"]
    RESULT["results_file on rank 0"]
    CLEANUP["backend_empty_cache(), barrier(), destroy_process_group()"]
    TEST --> WRAP
    WRAP --> ENV
    ENV --> DEVICE
    DEVICE --> GROUP
    GROUP --> CALL
    CALL --> REDUCE
    REDUCE --> RESULT
    RESULT --> CLEANUP
```

The wrapper sets distributed environment values, initializes the process group, runs the test function, aggregates rank failures, writes the result on rank 0, and performs cleanup and process-group destruction. [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:142-184]()

Sources: [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:15-48](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:66-111](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:114-139](), [tests/test_fsdp_mixin.py:142-184]()

# Page: Accelerate & Device Mapping

# Accelerate & Device Mapping

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes the Transformers model-loading integration points for Accelerate-based device dispatch, automatic device maps, memory-aware placement, and CPU or disk offload. The available source excerpts identify loading configuration fields and functions imported by `modeling_utils.py`, but do not include the implementations of those imported functions. Consequently, this page documents the visible interfaces without asserting details of their internal algorithms or execution order. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

---

## 1. Overview of Device Mapping

`modeling_utils.py` imports device-map and offload helpers from `transformers.integrations.accelerate`: `_get_device_map`, `check_and_set_device_map`, `accelerate_dispatch`, `accelerate_disk_offload`, `expand_device_map`, `get_device`, and `load_offloaded_parameter`. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74]()

The loading configuration includes `device_map`, `disk_offload_folder`, and `offload_buffers`, alongside dtype and checkpoint-related options. The field visible in this configuration is named `disk_offload_folder`; the available excerpt does not show whether or how a public `offload_folder` argument is translated into it. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

| Concern | Code entity | What the available source establishes |
|---|---|---|
| Load-time device assignment | `LoadStateDictConfig.device_map` | The configuration has an optional dictionary field for a device map. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]() |
| Disk offload configuration | `LoadStateDictConfig.disk_offload_folder` | The configuration has an optional path field for disk offload. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]() |
| Buffer offload option | `LoadStateDictConfig.offload_buffers` | The configuration has a boolean field, defaulting to `False`. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]() |
| Device-map handling | `check_and_set_device_map`, `_get_device_map`, `expand_device_map` | These functions are imported into `modeling_utils.py` from `integrations.accelerate`. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74]() |
| Dispatch and offload | `accelerate_dispatch`, `accelerate_disk_offload`, `load_offloaded_parameter` | These functions are imported into `modeling_utils.py` from `integrations.accelerate`. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74]() |

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

## 2. Implementation Architecture & Configuration

### `LoadStateDictConfig`

`LoadStateDictConfig` is a frozen dataclass declared in `modeling_utils.py`. Its visible fields include the pretrained model identifier, download options, safetensors selection, mismatch handling, sharded metadata, device map, disk-offload folder, buffer-offload flag, and dtype settings. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

| Field | Declared type/default | Role established by the field and declaration |
|---|---|---|
| `device_map` | `dict \| None = None` | Carries an optional device-map dictionary in the loading configuration. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]() |
| `disk_offload_folder` | `str \| None = None` | Carries an optional disk-offload path. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]() |
| `offload_buffers` | `bool = False` | Carries a buffer-offload setting. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]() |
| `dtype` | `torch.dtype \| None = None` | Carries an optional target dtype. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]() |
| `sharded_metadata` | `dict \| None = None` | Carries optional sharded-checkpoint metadata. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]() |

The available source shows these configuration fields and the helper imports, but not the code that populates the configuration, validates device-map values, derives memory budgets, or invokes dispatch. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:168-184]()

### Accelerate integration boundary

`modeling_utils.py` imports the device-map and offload helpers from `transformers.integrations.accelerate`. It also imports `add_hook_to_module` from `accelerate.hooks` only when Accelerate is available. These lines establish the dependencies, but do not expose hook types, hook behavior, or the dispatch call sites. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:140-143]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:140-143]()

## 4. Offloading and Weight-Loading Context

The loading configuration contains `disk_offload_folder` and `offload_buffers`; the Accelerate integration imports `accelerate_disk_offload` and `load_offloaded_parameter`. These declarations establish that disk offload and parameter loading are represented in the loading interfaces. They do not specify storage layout, file format, lazy-load timing, or CPU-offload behavior. [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:66-74](), [src/transformers/modeling_utils.py:175-184]()

The loading code also imports `offload_weight` from `transformers.integrations.accelerate` in `core_model_loading.py`. This identifies a weight-offload helper in the checkpoint-loading subsystem, but the available excerpt does not show its implementation or call sites. [src/transformers/core_model_loading.py:31-38]()

The visible code establishes model-loading interfaces for device mapping and disk offload: `LoadStateDictConfig` carries `device_map`, `disk_offload_folder`, and `offload_buffers`, while `modeling_utils.py` imports mapping, dispatch, and offload helpers from `transformers.integrations.accelerate`. The available excerpts do not include the helper implementations, so they do not support detailed claims about automatic map inference, balanced-memory heuristics, dispatch ordering, or runtime offload hooks. # Page: Pipeline Parallelism

# Pipeline Parallelism

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

Section 8.4 describes the codebase’s naive 1D pipeline-parallel path: splitting a model across sequential pipeline stages, communicating activations and gradients between stages, replacing non-local layers with identity stubs, and making final logits available beyond the last stage. The distributed configuration exposes pipeline parallelism through `pp_size`, and `DistributedMixin` delegates application of the pipeline transformation to `apply_pipeline_parallelism`. [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-28,54-56,67-77]() [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:34-39]()

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-28,54-56,67-77`; `src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:34-39`

---

## 1. Core Abstractions: `PipelineStage` and `PipelineIdentityLayer`

### Overview

`PipelineStage` represents a rank’s place in a linear pipeline. A stage holds the model components assigned to that rank and participates in activation and gradient communication with adjacent stages. The pipeline implementation also defines `PipelineIdentityLayer`, an identity stub used for layers that are not computed on the current rank, preserving the model’s module structure while the pipeline is partitioned. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

Pipeline parallelism is configured alongside tensor and FSDP parallelism. `DistributedConfig.pp_size` is the number of devices assigned to pipeline parallelism; it defaults to 1 when omitted. [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-28,54-56,67-77,106-116]()

`DistributedMixin` maintains a model’s pipeline plan in `_pp_plan`. During `init_parallel_plans`, it copies the class-level plan, merges the base-model plan from the model configuration, and incorporates plans declared by child modules. The `pp_plan` property exposes the resulting plan, and its setter accepts either a dictionary or `None`. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:58-69,79-104,120-122,157-165]()

### Diagram: Pipeline Ranks and Implementation Entities

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Natural_Language_Space"
        First["First pipeline rank"]
        Middle["Intermediate pipeline rank"]
        Last["Last pipeline rank"]
    end
    subgraph "Code_Entity_Space"
        StageFirst["PipelineStage(pp_rank=0)"]
        Stub["PipelineIdentityLayer"]
        StageMiddle["PipelineStage(pp_rank=1)"]
        StageLast["PipelineStage(pp_rank=pp_size-1)"]
        Apply["apply_pipeline_parallelism"]
    end
    First --> StageFirst
    Middle --> Stub
    Middle --> StageMiddle
    Last --> StageLast
    Apply --> StageFirst
    Apply --> StageMiddle
    Apply --> StageLast
```

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`; `src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:34-39`

---

## 2. Inter-Stage Communication and Data Flow

### Forward and Backward Flow

In a 1D pipeline, stages execute in model order. The first stage begins with the model input; each subsequent stage receives activations from its predecessor, performs its assigned computation, and forwards the resulting activations. During backward computation, gradients travel in the reverse direction. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

`PipelineStage.communicate` handles communication across stage boundaries. The first and last stages have only one neighboring stage, so communication in the direction beyond the pipeline boundary is skipped. Communication uses asynchronous distributed send and receive operations, with the method waiting for the relevant operations to complete. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

This is a naive stage-by-stage pipeline: the implementation described here does not establish a schedule that overlaps multiple microbatches. Its core data flow is the transfer of activations forward and gradients backward between neighboring stages. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

### Diagram: Stage-to-Stage Data Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Rank0 as "PipelineStage(pp_rank=0)"
    participant Rank1 as "PipelineStage(pp_rank=1)"
    participant Last as "PipelineStage(pp_rank=pp_size-1)"
    Rank0->>Rank0: "Compute local forward layers"
    Rank0->>Rank1: "Send forward activations"
    Rank1->>Rank1: "Receive activations and compute local layers"
    Rank1->>Last: "Forward activations through later stage(s)"
    Last->>Last: "Compute final local forward layers"
    Last-->>Rank1: "Send backward gradients"
    Rank1-->>Rank0: "Propagate gradients to preceding stage"
```

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`

---

## 3. Identity Layer Stubs and Checkpoint Placement

`PipelineIdentityLayer` is an identity module used where a layer is not owned by the current pipeline stage. It passes its input through without performing the replaced layer’s computation. Keeping stubs in the module structure allows the distributed model representation to retain the expected layer positions while computation is partitioned across ranks. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

The pipeline implementation also provides `PipelineStage.find_rank_for_key` for associating checkpoint keys with pipeline ranks. This supports determining which stage owns a model component when loading or saving a partitioned model. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

### Diagram: Model Layers, Stubs, and Stage Ownership

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["Input"]
    Embed["Embedding"]
    Layer0["Transformer layer 0"]
    Stub0["PipelineIdentityLayer stub"]
    Layer1["Transformer layer 1"]
    Stub1["PipelineIdentityLayer stub"]
    Layer2["Transformer layer 2"]
    Head["LM head"]
    Stage0["PipelineStage(pp_rank=0)"]
    Stage1["PipelineStage(pp_rank=1)"]
    Stage2["PipelineStage(pp_rank=2)"]
    Input --> Embed
    Embed --> Layer0
    Layer0 --> Stub0
    Stub0 --> Layer1
    Layer1 --> Stub1
    Stub1 --> Layer2
    Layer2 --> Head
    Stage0 -. "owns" .-> Embed
    Stage0 -. "owns" .-> Layer0
    Stage1 -. "owns" .-> Layer1
    Stage2 -. "owns" .-> Layer2
    Stage2 -. "owns" .-> Head
```

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`

---

## 4. Logits Broadcast and Final Output

The final pipeline stage computes the model’s final output logits. `PipelineStage.broadcast_from_last` broadcasts those logits from the last pipeline rank so that other ranks can access the output. When pipeline parallelism is not active, the method returns the logits without requiring a pipeline broadcast. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

This output step is distinct from the neighbor-to-neighbor activation transfers: activations move along the pipeline as computation advances, while the final logits are broadcast from the last stage to the other pipeline ranks. [src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200]()

### Diagram: From Input to Broadcast Logits

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["Model input"]
    First["PipelineStage(pp_rank=0)"]
    Communicate["PipelineStage.communicate"]
    Middle["Intermediate PipelineStage"]
    Final["PipelineStage(pp_rank=pp_size-1)"]
    Logits["Final logits"]
    Broadcast["PipelineStage.broadcast_from_last"]
    Outputs["Logits available on pipeline ranks"]
    Input --> First
    First --> Communicate
    Communicate --> Middle
    Middle --> Communicate
    Communicate --> Final
    Final --> Logits
    Logits --> Broadcast
    Broadcast --> Outputs
```

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`

---

## 5. Distributed Configuration and Integration

`DistributedConfig` includes `pp_size` as the pipeline-parallel size. The configuration resolver defaults it to 1 when unset, making the pipeline dimension inactive by default. The configuration also documents pipeline size as part of native distributed inference and training configuration. [src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-28,54-56,67-77,106-116]()

`DistributedMixin` imports `apply_pipeline_parallelism` from `distributed.pipeline_parallel`, alongside the tensor-parallel and FSDP application functions. This makes pipeline parallelism part of the distributed model orchestration layer. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:34-39]()

A model’s `_pp_plan` is assembled from class-level declarations, base-model configuration, and child-module contributions. The public `pp_plan` getter exposes that merged plan; the setter stores a dictionary, or clears the plan when passed `None`. [src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:58-69,79-104,120-122,157-165]()

### Diagram: Configuration and Transformation Path

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Config["DistributedConfig.pp_size"]
    Resolve["DistributedConfig._resolve_parallelism"]
    Mixin["DistributedMixin"]
    Plan["DistributedMixin._pp_plan"]
    Apply["apply_pipeline_parallelism"]
    Stage["PipelineStage"]
    Stubs["PipelineIdentityLayer"]
    Config --> Resolve
    Resolve --> Mixin
    Mixin --> Plan
    Plan --> Apply
    Apply --> Stage
    Apply --> Stubs
```

Sources: `src/transformers/distributed/configuration_utils.py:25-28,54-56,67-77,102-116`; `src/transformers/distributed/mixin.py:34-39,58-69,79-104,120-122,157-165`; `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`

---

## 6. Tests and Coverage Boundaries

The supplied test excerpt in `tests/tensor_parallel/test_tensor_parallel.py` includes an assertion that a loaded causal language model has an `lm_head` entry in `_pp_plan`. This verifies the presence of a class-level pipeline-plan entry and its preservation on the model instance alongside the tensor-parallel plan. The excerpt is a tensor-parallel test, not a direct test of stage communication or logits broadcast. [tests/tensor_parallel/test_tensor_parallel.py:135-145]()

The supplied excerpts do not show dedicated pipeline-parallel tests exercising `PipelineStage.communicate`, `PipelineIdentityLayer`, or `broadcast_from_last`. Consequently, those behaviors are described here from the pipeline implementation reference, while the test evidence shown is limited to the `_pp_plan` assertion. [tests/tensor_parallel/test_tensor_parallel.py:135-145]()

Sources: `tests/tensor_parallel/test_tensor_parallel.py:135-145`; `src/transformers/distributed/pipeline_parallel.py:1-200`

# Page: Attention Backends & Kernel Integration

# Attention Backends & Kernel Integration

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



This page introduces two related extension points: model-level attention backend dispatch and optional kernel substitutions for model operations. The attention interface selects an implementation for an attention layer; hub kernels can replace selected module forwards or functions with implementations loaded through the kernels integration.
Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-125]()

For details, see the child pages:
- [Flash Attention, SDPA & FlexAttention](#9.1) — attention implementations, the `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS` registry, and paged variants.
- [Hub Kernels & Custom Kernel Loading](#9.2) — `hub_kernels.py`, `@use_kernel_forward_from_hub`, kernel configuration, and hardware integrations.

---

## Pluggable Attention Architecture

The `transformers` library provides a pluggable attention system that allows models to select from various optimized attention implementations. Model code can import `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS` alongside its own attention implementation, separating model-specific projections and inputs from the selected attention backend. For example, the GPT-NeoX model utilizes this registry.
Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_neox/modeling_gpt_neox.py:25-26]()

The `sdpa_attention_forward` function, part of the SDPA integration, handles concerns such as grouped-query attention, causal behavior, and paged-cache updates before calling into the specific attention implementation.
Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-128]()

Flash Attention support includes compatibility metadata for multiple versions, devices, and kernel fallback repositories, managed by `modeling_flash_attention_utils.py`. For implementation selection and backend-specific behavior, see [Flash Attention, SDPA & FlexAttention](#9.1).
Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94]()

### Attention Dispatch: Concepts to Code Entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Model["Model attention layer"]
    Registry["ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS"]
    SDPA["sdpa_attention_forward"]
    Flash["flash_attention_forward"]
    Compatibility["FLASH_ATTENTION_COMPATIBILITY_MATRIX"]
    Model --> Registry
    Registry --> SDPA
    Registry --> Flash
    Flash --> Compatibility
```
Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_neox/modeling_gpt_neox.py:25-26]()[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-96]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:40-40]()[src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-100]()

---

## Hub-Loaded Custom Kernels

The hub-kernel integration provides mechanisms to dynamically load and use optimized kernels from the Hugging Face Hub. This is exposed through wrappers like `use_kernel_forward_from_hub` and `use_kernelized_func`. If hub kernels are disabled via the `USE_HUB_KERNELS` environment variable, these wrappers will issue a warning and return a no-op decorator, effectively bypassing the kernel integration.
Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-63]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-125]()

The default kernel mapping is built lazily, meaning that importing the `transformers` library does not immediately construct kernel repositories. Instead, repository setup is deferred until kernel usage is explicitly requested.
Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:139-145]()

Models can apply this extension point to selected modules. For instance, the GPT-OSS model decorates its `GptOssRMSNorm` with `@use_kernel_forward_from_hub("RMSNorm")` and `GptOssMLP` with `@use_kernel_forward_from_hub("MegaBlocksMoeMLP")` to leverage optimized kernel implementations for these components.
Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:46-47]()[src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-139]() For details on configuration, kernel loading, and hardware-specific integrations, see [Hub Kernels & Custom Kernel Loading](#9.2).

### Hub Kernel Integration: Concepts to Code Entities

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Model["GPT-OSS model code"]
    RMS["GptOssRMSNorm"]
    MLP["GptOssMLP"]
    Decorator["@use_kernel_forward_from_hub"]
    Wrapper["use_kernel_forward_from_hub"]
    Env["USE_HUB_KERNELS"]
    Mapping["_build_kernel_mapping"]
    Repository["LayerRepository"]
    Model --> RMS
    Model --> MLP
    RMS --> Decorator
    MLP --> Decorator
    Decorator --> Wrapper
    Env --> Wrapper
    Wrapper --> Mapping
    Mapping --> Repository
```
Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:46-47]()[src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-139]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-63]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:83-95]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-115]()[src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:139-153]()

---

- [Hub Kernels & Custom Kernel Loading](#9.2)

# Flash Attention, SDPA & FlexAttention

## Purpose and scope

This page covers the attention-backend integration points in the supplied material: Flash Attention compatibility metadata and lazy-import state, the SDPA wrapper’s cache and GQA handling, FlexAttention compilation helpers, and model-side references to `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS`. It also records the supplied Flash Attention CI workflow. The available material does not include the registry definition, the full Flash Attention or SDPA implementations, or paged backend modules, so details requiring those files are not inferred here. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-177](); [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:20-143](); [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:42-127](); [src/transformers/models/gpt_neox/modeling_gpt_neox.py:15-30](); [.github/workflows/self-scheduled-flash-attn-caller.yml:1-67]()

## 1. The Attention Registry and Selection

### `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS` Registry

Model code imports `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS` from `modeling_utils`; for example, GPT-NeoX imports it alongside `PreTrainedModel`. The supplied excerpt does not show the registry’s definition, registered backend keys, or a model call site that selects and invokes a registered function. [src/transformers/models/gpt_neox/modeling_gpt_neox.py:25-30]()

Accordingly, this page treats `ALL_ATTENTION_FUNCTIONS` as a model-facing registry reference, but does not assert its exact contents or selection behavior. The available backend excerpts define `sdpa_attention_forward`, `compile_friendly_flex_attention`, and Flash Attention compatibility and lazy-import helpers. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-96](); [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:58-126](); [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-177]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/models/gpt_neox/modeling_gpt_neox.py:25-30](), [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-96](), [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:58-126](), [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-177]()`


### Paged variants

The SDPA wrapper accepts an optional `PagedAttentionCache`. When the cache has that type, `sdpa_attention_forward` calls its `update` method with key/value states, the module’s `layer_idx`, and `kwargs` before continuing with GQA handling. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-123]()

The supplied excerpts do not show `split_attention_implementation`, paged backend registration, or the `flash_paged` and `sdpa_paged` modules. They therefore do not establish how paged backend names are parsed or how kernels consume page tables. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-123]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-123]()`

## 2. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA)

`sdpa_attention_forward` is defined in `src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py`. Its parameters include the attention module, query/key/value tensors, optional attention mask, dropout, optional scaling and causality settings, position bias, an optional `PagedAttentionCache`, and additional keyword arguments. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-96]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-96]()`


### Key mechanics

- **Paged-cache update:** If `cache` is a `PagedAttentionCache`, the wrapper calls `cache.update` before GQA handling. The update receives `key_states`, `value_states`, `module.layer_idx`, and `kwargs`. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:107-123]()
- **Grouped-query attention:** `use_gqa_in_sdpa` can force native GQA through `TRANSFORMERS_SDPA_FORCE_GQA=1`; it also uses device- and version-dependent conditions. If native GQA is not selected, `repeat_kv` expands key/value heads; otherwise, the wrapper sets `enable_gqa=True` in its SDPA keyword arguments. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:20-41](); [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:116-123]()
- **Position-bias masks:** `create_position_bias_mask` combines position bias with causal or supplied masks into a contiguous floating-point mask. For boolean masks, disallowed positions receive the minimum representable value for the key dtype; for additive masks, the mask is added to the position bias. The function warns that such masks usually prevent dispatch to the most efficient SDPA kernels. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:44-81]()
- **Unsupported options:** The wrapper raises `ValueError` when `softcap` is supplied and warns when `output_attentions=True`, noting that this SDPA path does not support returning attention weights. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:97-105]()
- **Causality setup:** The wrapper uses an explicit `is_causal` argument when provided, otherwise it falls back to `module.is_causal` and then `True`. The excerpt documents constraints on when SDPA Flash Attention and cuDNN kernels can rely on this flag, but does not include the subsequent final call. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:124-143]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:20-143]()`


### SDPA preparation workflow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["sdpa_attention_forward"] --> B{"softcap supplied?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C["raise ValueError"]
    B -->|"no"| D{"output_attentions requested?"}
    D -->|"yes"| E["warning_once"]
    D -->|"no"| F{"cache is PagedAttentionCache?"}
    E --> F
    F -->|"yes"| G["cache.update"]
    F -->|"no"| H["GQA decision"]
    G --> H
    H -->|"native GQA"| I["set enable_gqa"]
    H -->|"repeat heads"| J["repeat_kv for key and value"]
    I --> K["resolve is_causal"]
    J --> K
```

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:84-143]()`


## 3. Flash Attention Integration

`modeling_flash_attention_utils.py` contains Flash Attention availability helpers, compatibility metadata for versions 2, 3, and 4, fallback repository mappings, and shared module-level state for lazily loaded functions. The supplied excerpt does not include the body of `_lazy_imports` or the full implementation of `_flash_attention_forward`, so kernel invocation and tensor preprocessing details are not described here. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:43-177]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:43-177]()`


### Compatibility and fallback metadata

- `is_flash_attn_available` reports availability if Flash Attention 2, 3, or 4 is available, or if the NPU or XPU platform checks succeed. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:53-62]()
- `FLASH_ATTN_KERNEL_FALLBACK` maps version-specific backend names to Hub repository identifiers, including ROCm-specific alternatives for versions 2 and 3. `FLASH_ATTN_KERNEL_VERSIONS` records repository versions, while `FLASH_ATTN_KERNEL_DEVICES` lists device types for selected repositories. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94]()
- `FLASH_ATTENTION_COMPATIBILITY_MATRIX` stores per-version availability checks, package checks, and supported-device metadata. The shown entries describe Flash Attention versions 2, 3, and 4. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:96-146]()
- Module-level variables such as `_loaded_implementation`, `_flash_fn`, `_flash_varlen_fn`, and `_flash_with_kvcache_fn` are initialized to `None` for later loading. The excerpt also defines name mappings for differences between Hugging Face and Flash Attention keyword arguments. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:149-166]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:53-166]()`

## 4. Flex Attention

`integrations/flex_attention.py` conditionally imports PyTorch’s `BlockMask`, `create_block_mask`, and `flex_attention` when FlexAttention is available. The module checks the PyTorch version to determine whether the auxiliary-request API is available. [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:31-53]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:31-53]()`


### Compilation and auxiliary outputs

- **`WrappedFlexAttention`:** This singleton stores a compiled FlexAttention callable. Its initialization compiles `flex_attention` when needed and recompiles if the training mode changes. For PyTorch 2.6.0 training, it selects `max-autotune-no-cudagraphs`; otherwise it uses the default `torch.compile` call. [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:58-95]()
- **`compile_friendly_flex_attention`:** This helper uses the compiled callable unless TorchDynamo is already compiling, in which case it calls the uncompiled `flex_attention` function. It forwards query, key, value, and keyword arguments. [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:111-126]()
- **`get_flex_attention_lse_kwargs`:** This helper adapts the request for log-sum-exp output to the installed PyTorch API: it returns an `AuxRequest(lse=True)` form for PyTorch 2.9 and later, and a `return_lse` boolean form for earlier versions. [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:97-109]()
- **Block-mask helper:** `make_flex_block_causal_mask` is marked deprecated in favor of mask primitives in `masking_utils.py`. The shown excerpt describes constructing a compressed `BlockMask` for packed or unpacked sequences and begins its mask preparation logic. [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:132-181]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:58-181]()`


### FlexAttention call path

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["compile_friendly_flex_attention"] --> B{"TorchDynamo compiling?"}
    B -->|"yes"| C["use flex_attention"]
    B -->|"no"| D["WrappedFlexAttention(training)"]
    D --> E{"compiled for current mode?"}
    E -->|"no"| F["torch.compile flex_attention"]
    E -->|"yes"| G["reuse compiled callable"]
    F --> H["invoke compiled callable"]
    G --> H
    C --> I["invoke uncompiled callable"]
```

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:58-95](), [src/transformers/integrations/flex_attention.py:111-126]()`


## 5. Paged Attention Variants & Continuous Batching

The supplied SDPA implementation imports `PagedAttentionCache` from `generation.continuous_batching.cache` and checks for that type in `sdpa_attention_forward`. When present, it updates the key/value state before the wrapper’s GQA decision. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:1-6](); [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:107-123]()

The cache implementation and the paged Flash Attention and SDPA backend modules were not included in the supplied file contents. Consequently, allocator structure, page-table layout, scheduling interactions, and paged-kernel behavior cannot be documented from the available evidence. [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:5-6](); [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:107-123]()

Sources: `[src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:1-6](), [src/transformers/integrations/sdpa_attention.py:107-123]()`


### Diagram: Paged Cache Update in SDPA

## 6. Flash Attention CI

The supplied self-scheduled Flash Attention workflow can be triggered by a repository dispatch, a daily schedule, pushes to branches matching `run_nvidia_ci_flash_attn*`, or manual dispatch. Manual inputs allow previous and comparison workflow run IDs; the setup job writes those values to artifacts. [`.github/workflows/self-scheduled-flash-attn-caller.yml:1-52]()

The `model-ci` job calls the reusable daily CI workflow with the `run_models_gpu` job, an A10 runner, and the `huggingface/transformers-all-latest-gpu:flash-attn` Docker image. Its pytest marker selects `flash_attn_test`, `flash_attn_3_test`, `flash_attn_4_test`, or `all_flash_attn_test`. This workflow demonstrates CI coverage and routing; it does not describe runtime backend selection or kernel implementation. [`.github/workflows/self-scheduled-flash-attn-caller.yml:55-68]()

Sources: `[.github/workflows/self-scheduled-flash-attn-caller.yml:1-67]()`


### Diagram: Flash Attention CI Routing

```mermaid

    B --> C["setup_values artifact"]
    A --> D["model-ci"]
    D --> E["daily-ci_reusable.yml"]
    E --> F["run_models_gpu"]
    F --> G["flash-attn Docker image"]
    F --> H["A10 runner"]
    F --> I["flash_attn_test / flash_attn_3_test / flash_attn_4_test / all_flash_attn_test"]
```

# Page: Hub Kernels & Custom Kernel Loading

# Hub Kernels & Custom Kernel Loading

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

This page describes how Transformers integrates kernels from the Hugging Face Hub and local repositories, how model modules opt into Hub-provided forwards, and how related attention and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) integrations select specialized implementations. The main entry points are `transformers.integrations.hub_kernels`, `transformers.utils.kernel_config`, and the integrations that connect kernels to attention and MoE code. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:15-20](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:20-29]()

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:15-20](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:20-29]()

---

## 1. Overview and Core Architecture

The Hub-kernel integration provides decorators and mapping support for replacing selected model forwards or functions with implementations supplied by the `kernels` package. The Transformers wrapper checks the `USE_HUB_KERNELS` environment variable: when Hub kernels are disabled, the decorators warn once and return an identity decorator rather than installing the underlying kernel behavior. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-64](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-137]()

When the `kernels` package is available, `hub_kernels.py` imports its repository classes and dispatch helpers, including `LayerRepository`, `LocalLayerRepository`, `replace_kernel_forward_from_hub`, and `get_kernel`. The module also contains internal function-name-to-module-path mappings for operations such as `selective_scan_fn` and `mamba_chunk_scan_combined`. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:66-77](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:83-105]()

The default kernel mapping is intentionally constructed lazily: `_KERNEL_MAPPING_CACHE` starts empty, and `_build_kernel_mapping()` is defined as the mapping builder. The module comments explain that this avoids constructing kernel repositories merely because Transformers or `transformers.pipeline` was imported; the repositories are intended to be created when kernel use is explicitly requested. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:139-146]()

### Diagram: Mapping Configuration and Kernel Decorator Path

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Env["USE_HUB_KERNELS"] --> Gate["_kernels_enabled"]
    Gate --> Decorator["use_kernel_forward_from_hub(layer_name)"]
    Decorator -->|enabled| Underlying["kernels.use_kernel_forward_from_hub"]
    Decorator -->|disabled| Identity["identity decorator"]
    Mapping["KernelConfig.kernel_mapping"] --> Validate["KernelConfig.sanitize_kernel_mapping(model)"]
    Validate --> Repositories["LayerRepository or LocalLayerRepository"]
    Lazy["get_kernel_mapping_transformers"] --> Build["_build_kernel_mapping()"]
    Build --> Repositories
    Underlying --> Forward["decorated module forward"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-64](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-114](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:139-146](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-89](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:131-149]()

### Natural-language concepts mapped to code entities

| System concept | Code entity | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Enable or disable Hub-kernel decorators | `_TRANSFORMERS_USE_HUB_KERNELS`, `_kernels_enabled` | Reads and evaluates `USE_HUB_KERNELS`. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-64]() |
| Decorate a module for a Hub forward | `use_kernel_forward_from_hub(layer_name)` | Delegates to the `kernels` decorator when enabled; otherwise returns an identity decorator. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-114]() |
| Describe a remote kernel repository | `LayerRepository` | Constructed with a repository ID, layer name, version, and optional revision and trust setting. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-70]() |
| Describe a local kernel repository | `LocalLayerRepository` | Constructed from a local path and layer name. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:73-89]() |
| Collect model layer names for mapping | `KernelConfig.store_registered_layer_names(model)` | Scans module kernel-function and kernel-layer metadata. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-129]() |

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-64](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-114](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-89](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-129]()

---

## 2. Core Decorators and APIs

`use_kernel_forward_from_hub(layer_name)` is the Transformers-facing class decorator. If `_kernels_enabled` is true, it returns the underlying `kernels.use_kernel_forward_from_hub(layer_name)` decorator. If disabled, it logs a warning once and returns a decorator that leaves the class unchanged. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-114]()

`use_kernelized_func(module_names)` handles function-based kernelization. It normalizes a single callable into a list, then passes the callables to the underlying `kernels.use_kernelized_func`; when Hub kernels are disabled, it follows the same warning-and-identity pattern. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:116-125]()

`use_kernel_func_from_hub(layer_name)` is retained as a deprecated wrapper. When enabled, it emits a deprecation warning and delegates to the underlying `kernels.use_kernel_forward_from_hub`; when disabled, it returns an identity decorator after warning about the environment setting. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:127-138]()

A model example is GPT-OSS: `GptOssRMSNorm` is decorated with `@use_kernel_forward_from_hub("RMSNorm")`, while `GptOssMLP` uses the `"MegaBlocksMoeMLP"` layer name. These declarations associate model module classes with kernel layer names; the ordinary class implementations remain present in the model file. [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:46-61](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-141]()

### Diagram: Decorator from Model Declaration to Transformers Wrapper

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Class["GptOssRMSNorm"] --> Decorator["use_kernel_forward_from_hub(\"RMSNorm\")"]
    Decorator --> Wrapper["transformers.integrations.hub_kernels.use_kernel_forward_from_hub"]
    Wrapper --> Gate{"_kernels_enabled"}
    Gate -->|true| KernelsDecorator["kernels.use_kernel_forward_from_hub"]
    Gate -->|false| Identity["identity decorator"]
    KernelsDecorator --> LayerName["layer_name = RMSNorm"]
    Identity --> ClassForward["GptOssRMSNorm.forward"]
    LayerName --> ClassForward
```

Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:46-61](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:62-64](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-114]()

Sources: [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:46-61](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-141](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:107-138]()

---

## 3. KernelConfig and Mapping Management

`KernelConfig` stores a model’s kernel mapping and related options. Its constructor accepts `kernel_mapping`, `use_local_kernel`, and `inherit_mapping`; it initializes `registered_layer_names` as an empty mapping. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:92-101]()

`infer_device(model)` determines the device type from the first model parameter. If the model has no parameters, it raises `ValueError` and asks the caller to provide a device in the mapping. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:22-48]()

The mapping helpers support two repository forms:

- `add_to_mapping(...)` checks that the device is in `KERNELS_SUPPORTED_DEVICE_TYPES`, parses `repo_name` as `org/repo:layer_name`, and adds a `LayerRepository` under the layer, device, and mode. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-70]()
- `add_to_mapping_local(...)` applies the same supported-device check and parses the repository string as a local path followed by `:layer_name`, then creates a `LocalLayerRepository`. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:73-89]()

`KernelConfig.update_kernel(...)` updates its mapping with a remote `LayerRepository`. The repository entry carries `repo_id`, `layer_name`, `revision`, `version`, and `trust_remote_code`. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:103-118]()

`store_registered_layer_names(model)` scans `model.named_modules()`. For modules with `_kernel_funcs`, it records each function kernel name under a qualified module name; for modules with `kernel_layer_name`, it records the module’s registered kernel layer name. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-129]()

`sanitize_kernel_mapping(model)` documents and validates mapping shape and compatibility: mapped layer names must correspond to registered model layers, device keys must be supported, and repository entries must follow remote or local naming formats. The accepted forms include a single-device mapping, per-device mappings, and values with metadata such as `version`, `revision`, or `trust_remote_code`. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:131-149](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:151-180]()

| Mapping concern | Relevant API or field | Implementation detail |
|---|---|---|
| Supported accelerator names | `KERNELS_SUPPORTED_DEVICE_TYPES` | Includes `cuda`, `rocm`, `xpu`, `npu`, `neuron`, `tpu`, and `mps`. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20]() |
| Remote repository mapping | `add_to_mapping`, `KernelConfig.update_kernel` | Builds `LayerRepository` entries. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-70](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:103-118]() |
| Local repository mapping | `add_to_mapping_local` | Builds `LocalLayerRepository` entries using a `Path`. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:73-89]() |
| Module-to-kernel registration | `store_registered_layer_names` | Reads `_kernel_funcs` and `kernel_layer_name` from model modules. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-129]() |
| Mapping validation | `sanitize_kernel_mapping` | Checks registered layer names, device names, repository formats, and metadata constraints. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:131-149]() |

### Diagram: `KernelConfig` Mapping Construction and Validation

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Model["model.named_modules()"] --> Store["KernelConfig.store_registered_layer_names(model)"]
    Store --> Registered["registered_layer_names"]
    Input["kernel_mapping"] --> Sanitize["KernelConfig.sanitize_kernel_mapping(model)"]
    Registered --> Sanitize
    Sanitize -->|remote org/repo:layer_name| Remote["add_to_mapping / LayerRepository"]
    Sanitize -->|local /abs/path:layer_name| Local["add_to_mapping_local / LocalLayerRepository"]
    Remote --> Mapping["KernelConfig.kernel_mapping"]
    Local --> Mapping
    Device["infer_device(model)"] --> DeviceType["get_device_type(param.device)"]
    DeviceType --> Mapping
```

Sources: [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:22-48](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-89](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:92-101](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-149]()

Sources: [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:22-48](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-89](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:92-101](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:120-149]()

---

## 4. DeepGEMM and SonicMoE Integrations

`transformers.integrations.moe` imports `deepgemm_bf16_experts_forward` from `deepgemm` and `sonicmoe_experts_forward` from `sonicmoe`. These are integrated alongside the generic MoE implementation, including `_batched_linear` and `batched_mm_experts_forward`. [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:27-29](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:78-117]()

The generic `batched_mm_experts_forward` flattens the token/expert routing into selected token states, routing weights, and expert IDs. It selects the corresponding expert projection weights, applies the up projection and gate or activation, then proceeds to the down projection path. For expert-parallel sentinel IDs, it clamps IDs for indexing and uses the sentinel mask to identify those entries. [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:112-159]()

`deepgemm.py` describes its integration as providing grouped GEMM entry points, including BF16 expert forward and FP8/FP4 linear and expert paths. Its documented requirements include CUDA, Hopper SM90 or newer, CUDA runtime 12.3 or newer, and `kernels-community/deep-gemm`; the Mega MoE path additionally requires SM100 or newer. The module defines a `DeepGEMM` dataclass containing the curated callable entry points and alignment metadata. [src/transformers/integrations/deepgemm.py:15-24](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepgemm.py:53-74]()

GPT-OSS illustrates two kernel-related extension points: `GptOssExperts` is decorated with `@use_experts_implementation(...)`, and `GptOssMLP` is decorated with `@use_kernel_forward_from_hub("MegaBlocksMoeMLP")`. The experts implementation stores projection weights as expert-indexed tensors and computes routed outputs; the decorators associate those model components with alternative implementations. [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:67-87](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:89-113](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-141]()

### Diagram: MoE Implementation Entry Points

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Routed["hidden_states, top_k_index, top_k_weights"] --> Batched["batched_mm_experts_forward"]
    Batched --> Select["expert_ids and selected weights"]
    Select --> Projection["_batched_linear"]
    Projection --> Gate["gate or activation"]
    Gate --> Down["down projection and routing weights"]
    Integrations["integrations.moe imports"] --> Deep["deepgemm_bf16_experts_forward"]
    Integrations --> Sonic["sonicmoe_experts_forward"]
    GPT["GptOssExperts"] --> ExpertsDecorator["use_experts_implementation"]
    GPT --> HubDecorator["use_kernel_forward_from_hub(\"MegaBlocksMoeMLP\")"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:27-29](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:78-109](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:112-159](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:67-113](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:132-141]()

Sources: [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:27-29](), [src/transformers/integrations/moe.py:78-159](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepgemm.py:15-24](), [src/transformers/integrations/deepgemm.py:53-74](), [src/transformers/models/gpt_oss/modeling_gpt_oss.py:67-141]()

---

## 5. Hardware and Platform Integrations

`KernelConfig` recognizes device types including CUDA, ROCm, XPU, NPU, Neuron, TPU, and MPS. The supported-device list is used by the mapping helpers to reject unsupported device keys. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:51-57](), [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:73-79]()

The Hub-kernel integration imports device and capability-related types from `kernels`, including `CUDAProperties` and `ROCMProperties`. Its default mapping builder includes a CUDA-specific `Qwen3_5GatedDeltaNet` entry constrained to compute capability 121, illustrating that mappings can be selected with hardware-property constraints. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:83-95](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:145-172]()

Flash Attention fallback metadata distinguishes ROCm from other platforms for FlashAttention 2 and 3. On ROCm, those variants point to `kernels-community/aiter-flash-attn`; otherwise, the mappings use CUDA-oriented repositories. The associated device metadata lists ROCm for the AITER repository and CUDA or XPU for other repositories as applicable. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94]()

Ascend NPU attention has a separate integration path in `npu_flash_attention.py`. It imports `npu_fusion_attention` when NPU support is available, uses `NPU_FA2_SPARSE_MODE` to select supported causal-mask alignment, and caches a causal attention mask per device. The NPU FlashAttention functions dispatch to `npu_fusion_attention` with the appropriate layout and sequence-length metadata. [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:18-48](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:51-83](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:86-143]()

| Platform or device | Integration point | Behavior represented in the provided code |
|---|---|---|
| CUDA | `CUDAProperties`, `Device` | A default mapping can constrain a kernel by CUDA capability. [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:145-172]() |
| ROCm | `is_rocm_platform()`, `aiter-flash-attn` | FlashAttention fallback repositories differ on ROCm; AITER is listed as ROCm-supported. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94]() |
| Ascend NPU | `npu_flash_attn_func`, `npu_flash_attn_varlen_func` | Uses `npu_fusion_attention`, device-cached masks, and configurable sparse-mask mode. [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:18-48](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:51-138]() |
| XPU and other listed types | `KERNELS_SUPPORTED_DEVICE_TYPES` | Included in the mapping configuration’s supported device names. [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20]() |

Sources: [src/transformers/utils/kernel_config.py:19-20](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:83-95](), [src/transformers/integrations/hub_kernels.py:145-172](), [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:18-48]()

---

## 6. FlashAttention and Operator Fallbacks

`modeling_flash_attention_utils.py` declares fallback repositories for FlashAttention 2, 3, and 4. FlashAttention 2 and 3 select the AITER repository on ROCm; FlashAttention 4 uses `kernels-community/flash-attn4`. The file also records versions and device support for the Hub repositories. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94]()

| Attention variant | Fallback repository | Device metadata |
|---|---|---|
| `flash_attention_2` | `kernels-community/aiter-flash-attn` on ROCm; otherwise `kernels-community/flash-attn2`. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:66-69]() | `aiter-flash-attn` is listed for ROCm; `flash-attn2` is listed for CUDA and XPU. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:86-94]() |
| `flash_attention_3` | `kernels-community/aiter-flash-attn` on ROCm; otherwise `kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3`. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:70-72]() | AITER is listed for ROCm; `vllm-flash-attn3` is listed for CUDA. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:86-94]() |
| `flash_attention_4` | `kernels-community/flash-attn4`. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:73]() | Listed for CUDA. [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:86-94]() |

The NPU FlashAttention implementation is distinct from those repository fallback mappings. It adapts the FlashAttention-style arguments to `npu_fusion_attention`; causal mode obtains a cached mask and passes `SPARSE_MODE`, while variable-length mode passes sequence lengths derived from cumulative sequence-length tensors. [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:37-48](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:51-83](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:86-138]()

Sources: [src/transformers/modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:64-94](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:37-48](), [src/transformers/integrations/npu_flash_attention.py:51-138]()

# Page: Pipelines

# Pipelines

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)

</details>



## Purpose and scope

The `pipeline()` API provides task-oriented entry points to model inference. The `Pipeline` base class and task registry connect pipeline implementations with supported tasks and model classes. This page summarizes that routing and the relationship between pipeline families; implementation details are covered in the child pages. [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:49-63](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

- For details on text generation, conversational inputs, chat templating, tool-call parsing, and streaming, see [Text & Conversational Pipelines](#10.1).
- For details on vision, audio, and multimodal tasks, see [Vision, Audio & Multimodal Pipelines](#10.2).

Sources: [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:49-63](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

---

### Core architecture and task routing

`Pipeline` is the shared base class for task-specific pipeline implementations. The pipelines package exposes the base class, the registry, and helpers such as `load_model`; it also imports the concrete pipeline classes that implement supported tasks. [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:49-63](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:64-90]()

The `SUPPORTED_TASKS` registry associates task names with an implementation class, supported PyTorch model classes, and, for the entries shown below, a default model and task type. `TASK_ALIASES` maps alternate names such as `sentiment-analysis` and `ner` to canonical task names. [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

**Diagram: Task registry connects task names to pipeline implementations**

```mermaid
graph LR
    task["Task name"] --> registry["SUPPORTED_TASKS"]
    registry --> impl["impl"]
    registry --> models["pt model classes"]
    registry --> default["default model"]
    alias["TASK_ALIASES"] --> canonical["Canonical task"]
    canonical --> registry
    impl -.-> cls["TextClassificationPipeline"]
    models -.-> auto["AutoModelForSequenceClassification"]
```

Sources: [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

### Pipeline execution and inputs

Pipeline implementations share a common base while specializing the task-specific handling of inputs and outputs. The base module imports model, tokenizer, processor, image-processor, and video-processor abstractions, and includes utilities for batching and padding inputs. [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:32-57](), [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:75-123](), [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:126-180]()

For example, `TextGenerationPipeline` accepts text prompts and conversational message lists, while `AutomaticSpeechRecognitionPipeline` handles audio input. These are separate task implementations under the shared pipeline interface. [src/transformers/pipelines/text_generation.py:23-28](), [src/transformers/pipelines/automatic_speech_recognition.py:146-168]()

**Diagram: User-facing tasks mapped to code entities**

```mermaid
graph TD
    textTask["text-generation"] --> textClass["TextGenerationPipeline"]
    textClass --> textFile["pipelines/text_generation.py"]
    audioTask["automatic-speech-recognition"] --> asrClass["AutomaticSpeechRecognitionPipeline"]
    asrClass --> asrFile["pipelines/automatic_speech_recognition.py"]
    audioGenTask["text-to-audio"] --> audioGenClass["TextToAudioPipeline"]
    audioGenClass --> audioGenFile["pipelines/text_to_audio.py"]
    registry["SUPPORTED_TASKS"] --> textClass
    registry --> asrClass
    registry --> audioGenClass
```

Sources: [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:49-63](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172](), [src/transformers/pipelines/text_generation.py:22-28](), [src/transformers/pipelines/automatic_speech_recognition.py:146-168](), [src/transformers/pipelines/text_to_audio.py:46-49]()

---

### Pipeline families

#### Text and conversational pipelines

Text-focused implementations include text generation, classification, and token classification. `TextGenerationPipeline` supports both text prompts and chat-form message lists; `pipeline()` routing connects task names to their implementations through the task registry. For details, see [Text & Conversational Pipelines](#10.1). [src/transformers/pipelines/text_generation.py:22-28](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:77-85](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

Sources: [src/transformers/pipelines/text_generation.py:22-28](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:77-85](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()

#### Vision, audio, and multimodal pipelines

The package also provides implementations for audio, vision, video, and multimodal tasks. Examples include `AutomaticSpeechRecognitionPipeline`, `TextToAudioPipeline`, `ImageTextToTextPipeline`, and `AnyToAnyPipeline`. For details, see [Vision, Audio & Multimodal Pipelines](#10.2). [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:49-51](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:64-90](), [src/transformers/pipelines/automatic_speech_recognition.py:146-168](), [src/transformers/pipelines/text_to_audio.py:46-49]()

### Summary

The pipeline system groups model inference behind a shared `Pipeline` base and task-specific implementations. The task registry connects task identifiers to those implementations and their supported model classes. Consult the child pages for modality-specific behavior and implementation detail. [src/transformers/pipelines/base.py:26-40](), [src/transformers/pipelines/__init__.py:134-172]()
